Name: Liberal Arts English Reading
College: Department of English Language and Literature
Prerequisite: University course on modularization in English
Introduction:
This course aims to improve students' English reading ability. Through students' extensive reading and teachers' teaching of reading skills and strategies, students' reading speed and comprehension ability are improved. _x000D_
This course uses three or four volumes of "Liberal Arts English" to enable students to read a large number of articles in multiple fields of the humanities in and out of class. Through teacher lectures and student discussions in class, students can develop their ability to summarize literature and think critically. At the same time, the selected texts consciously make cultural comparisons, allowing students to enhance their cross-cultural awareness while improving their English reading ability. _x000D_
The course has a final closed-book written examination, combined with multiple assessment methods such as classroom vocabulary tests, oral class reports, and text summary writing, in an effort to fairly evaluate students' learning results while supervising students' learning. _x000D_

Having a good foundation in mathematical analysis plays a key role in future study and research. _x000D_

Introduction: This course is mainly devoted to master-digit laws and centres. While demonstrating the classic theoretical conclusions, emphasis is placed on the application of these results in practical examples.

Name: Advanced Statistics
Introduction: This is a core course on statistical theory mainly offered to master's and doctoral students with an appropriate knowledge base in probability, statistics and related majors. Students should first take courses in mathematical statistics, probability theory and measure theory. Senior undergraduates can take this course as an elective.

Name: Analytical English Writing
College: Department of English Language and Literature
Introduction:
The "Academic English Writing" course is mainly taught to non-English major undergraduates at Peking University who have completed basic college English courses, have certain reading and writing abilities, and hope to understand analytical writing through systematic writing courses and corresponding training, especially the thinking, organization, writing and criticism skills required for current and future academic paper writing. The course uses a combination of studying academic literature and imitating writing to help students become familiar with the structure and patterns of academic writing through reading literature, and use this as a basis and reference for writing exercises, in order to fully understand and become familiar with academic writing paradigms from the whole to the details. _x000D_
The Academic Writing course focuses on the writing process as a way of discovering and developing ideas. That is to say, this course regards writing as a tool of thought - a way to carry out continuous exploration and reflection; specifically in the field of academic research, it is a logical reasoning process that clearly and effectively presents academic research results and continuously discovers and solves research problems in the writing process. _x000D_
Generally speaking, most people believe that writing is the mastery and application of a language form; therefore, special attention will be paid to the language mode of writing. But ultimately, language is only a carrier of ideas and content; therefore writing itself is more of a mental activity, and writing training should also be a kind of logical thinking training. By writing, we can figure out what we are talking about. The act and process of writing allows us to discover and explore what we think and believe. This is the analytical nature of writing, and it is also the primary premise and foundation of academic writing. _x000D_

Name: Topics in Representation Theory

Name: Selected Topics in Modular Forms
Prerequisite: Linear algebras, abstract algebras, solid analysis, complex analysis and primary numerics.
Introduction:
A result called the modularity theorem is expressed as: _x000D_
_x000D_
     All rational elliptic curves are modular forms. _x000D_
_x000D_
For a large class of elliptic curves, this theorem was proved by Wiles. One of the key technologies was completed by Wiles and Taylor. As a result, 350 years later, Fermat's last theorem was finally perfectly proved. Later, the entire modularity theorem was proved by Breuil, Conrad, Taylor and Diamond. _x000D_
_x000D_
There are many versions of the modularity theorem, and they touch all aspects of mathematics: analysis, algebra, geometry and number theory. Starting from the basic concepts of modular forms, this course will explain the relationship between different versions of the modularity theorem. _x000D_
_x000D_
Students are required to have studied linear algebra, abstract algebra, real analysis, complex analysis and elementary number theory. The main reference is: "A First Course in Modular Forms" by Diamond and Shurman, GTM 228._x000D_

Name: Infinity Categories
Introduction: This course mainly introduces the background knowledge and basic theory of infinite categories, including: model category, homotopy algebra, fibration of simplex and stable infinite categories, etc. The infinite category is the basic language for establishing and deriving algebraic geometry, and is also one of the basic tools of geometric representation theory. It is used by Lurie and Gaitsgory to prove the Weil conjecture about Tamagawa numbers in the function field, and is also used by Bahtt, Morrow, Scholze and others to establish p-adic Hodge theory. Recently, infinite categories have also been used to study algebraic K-theory.

Name: Roman History
Introduction: Like ancient Greek civilization, ancient Roman civilization was an integral part of the overall economic, political and cultural development of the ancient Mediterranean region. In this region, the Romans, who arose as a city-state in central Italy, later became politically dominant in the form of the Roman Empire. The evolution of Roman civilization was prominently based on its institutions, and the growth of its politics, laws, and various institutions was characterized by improvement and gradualism. Ancient Rome's literary and artistic achievements were impressive, but a closer examination still reveals the indelible influence of its political and legal systems. The origin of Christianity and its eventual becoming the official religion of the empire impacted traditional concepts and institutions to a certain extent. However, the Christian church itself also experienced a process of mutual adaptation and integration with the Roman political and legal system. The study of Roman history has a rich and long doctrinal history. The teaching, reading and discussion of this course will pay attention to tracing the previous academic views and debates on important issues in Roman history.

Name: Software Programming for Financial Engineering
Prerequisite: The course is a relatively advanced elective course on finance and programming. Students taking the course should have background in finance, mathematics and programming. On the finance side, students are expected to grasp concepts such as risk premium, stochastic discount rate, no arbitrage, equilibrium asset pricing models (Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)). Calculus, linear algebra and probability are required. Basic understanding of stochastic process is useful but not required. Prior programming experience of C or Python or etc is required.
Introduction:
It is very common to use software such as MATLAB to process data and calculations in modern financial engineering. This course mainly teaches computer programming_x000D_
Application of fixed income securities and derivatives pricing, asset portfolio calculation, and multi-factor stock pricing models in financial engineering. The purpose is to enable senior undergraduate students to become familiar with current theoretical models of financial engineering and become proficient in using software to deal with practical software programming problems in financial engineering through this course. _x000D_

Name: Applied Time Series Analysis
Introduction: This course introduces students to time series models and the application of these models to economic and financial data. This course will introduce linear models in detail, and nonlinear models will also be covered. We will first introduce the traditional time series method - ARMA model in detail, then dynamic modeling and regression methods, and also introduce nonlinear models, such as autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity and threshold autoregressive models. In addition, tools commonly used in time series models in finance and economics in recent years, such as cointegration, error correction models, and vector autoregressive models, will also be covered. We not only study the statistical models themselves, but more importantly focus on their application to real-world data. Since this is an applied time series course, we will cover quite a few examples.

Name: Stochastic Analysis and Applications
Prerequisite: calculus, linear algebra, probability theory, statistics
Introduction: Stochastic analysis has become an important research tool in many areas of science and technology. For example, academic research in quantitative analysis and trading in financial institutions or in dynamic asset pricing are based on stochastic models. This course first introduces the main theories and tools of stochastic analysis, and then discusses the applications of stochastic analysis in different fields, especially economics and finance. For those students who are interested in doing academic research, this course will provide solid research tools for pricing financial derivatives and establishing optimal investment portfolios, two important research directions in the field of financial economics. This course will also provide the necessary technical preparation for students who wish to work in quantitative research and trading at buy-side or sell-side institutions in the financial industry.

Name: Financial Economics
Introduction: “Financial Economics” is an introductory course on finance for financial beginners. The course presents the main elements of the current mainstream of financial economics to the extent acceptable to undergraduate students, highlighting the financial thinking behind the theory. The course consists mainly of three main components: balanced asset pricing; arbitrage asset pricing; and financial friction. The balanced asset-pricing component will introduce the theory of decision-making in an environment of rational human uncertainty, the portfolio theory, and theories such as CAPM, C-CAPM to balance asset-pricing in order to develop a holistic understanding of financial operations. In the arbitrage asset-pricing section, theories such as the basic theorem of asset-pricing, risk neutral pricing, dynamic hedges will be introduced to outline the theoretical foundations of the development of contemporary derivative financial markets. In the financial friction section, theories such as credit rations, financial contracts, the Diamond-Dybvig Bank Model, the financial crisis, etc. will be introduced to analyse the underlying rationale behind important financial phenomena, including the subprime crisis. Most of these are analyses of financial problems within a rational framework. Finally, the course will briefly address the theory of behavioural finance and explore the impact of some widespread behavioural biases on financial operations. The introduction of knowledge of financial theory is an important teaching objective of the course, but not all. The more important objective of the course is to develop an in-depth understanding of key financial phenomena, ranging from sensory to rational, and to be able to use theory to guide financial decision-making, through the teaching of financial literacy, so that students can understand the patterns behind real world financial operations. This course is preceded by the 2015 spring course, Theory of Finance and Financial Markets (2 credits) and the 2016 spring course, Theory of Finance (3 credits). Starting in 2017, the number of course credits was increased to four to cover more fully the area of financial knowledge. The title of the course has also been changed to " Financial Economics " to reflect the financial introductory nature of the course. Taking into account that the background of the students attending this course may vary widely and the mathematical base may vary widely, in order to make the course as suitable as possible for the taste of different students, the course contains both study and content enhancement components. The study was the subject of the course and the scope of the normal course and the mid-term final examination. The content of the study is designed to present the idea of financial economics in a more straightforward and straightforward mathematical language, and the level of difficulty should be suitable for a wide range of students, including academics. In addition, the course contains a number of technical enhancements (e.g. the extrapolation of the Black-Scholes formula). These are taught in the classroom in order to broaden the eyes of the students, but they are not required in homework and examinations. While the course will try to be as accessible as possible in terms of mathematical requirements, it cannot be downgraded because contemporary financial economics itself is a highly mathematical discipline with distinct quantitative features. Students who have asked to take this course have taken both linear algebra and econometric courses, or have an equal stock of mathematical knowledge. This course does not require students to have taken other financial courses but has already completed secondary microeconomics.

This type of model is mainly derived from stochastic differential equations and diffusion processes with jumps. Its main applications in quantitative finance include risk-neutral pricing theory, option pricing, exotic option pricing, and pricing standard conversion, etc. Students who complete this course should possess the basic knowledge and operational techniques of stochastic calculus and its related applications in quantitative finance.

Name: Economics and Computation
College: School of Electronics Engineering and Computer Science
Prerequisite: The course only requires basic knowledge in algorithms. No background in Economics is necessary.
Introduction: Economics and computing (non-computational economics) are emerging popular interdisciplinary subjects in recent years. It covers economics, theoretical computer science, and artificial intelligence. This course will provide a step-by-step introduction to the field of economics and computing, explaining relevant economic principles (including the core work of more than a dozen Nobel Prize winners in economics), algorithm theory, computational thinking, and artificial intelligence (including algorithmic game theory and computational social choice theory). We will discuss in detail some key algorithms, protocols, and popular applications such as crowdsourcing and Bitcoin.

Name: Applied Partial Differential Equations
Prerequisite: Mathematic analysis (high math), upper algebra (linear algebra), mathematical physical equation, multiple function
Introduction:
Partial differential equations play an important role in almost all fields of science. This class focuses on the solution of partial differential equations, _x000D_

Name: Labor Economics
Introduction: This course is aimed at senior economics undergraduate students. It teaches the basic theories of labor economics, introduces classic literature, and uses econometric methods to analyze issues related to labor economics. Including labor supply, labor demand, immigration, wages, human capital, returns to education, health, aging and social security.

Name: Risk Theory
Introduction: This course will introduce the nature and modeling methods of collective risk models, discuss the basic models and conclusions of ruin theory, discuss several basic concepts and conclusions of risk decision-making and risk measurement, and further risk exchange issues, and finally briefly introduce the application of the martingale process in risk theory.

Name: Game Theory
Introduction: This course is an introductory game theory course for senior undergraduates. It aims to provide students with a comprehensive and systematic game theory training and cultivate students' strategic thinking. Through the study of this course, students can have the basic ability to apply game theory to analyze economics and other social science issues. The course contents include static games with complete information, dynamic games with complete information, static games with incomplete information and dynamic games with incomplete information.

Name: Advanced Econometrics II
Introduction:
As a continuation of Econometrics I, this course focuses on introducing microeconometrics and its application in empirical studies, mainly involving related methods and applications such as discrete data, limited dependent variables, and panel data. The course introduces the estimation and inference of cross-sectional data models where the dependent variables are discrete data and truncated and censored data. It then introduces linear panel data static models and dynamic models, and provides a preliminary introduction to treatment effects, spatial correlation models, etc. _x000D_
_x000D_
This course requires students to have enough time after class to digest the content and read the listed literature to enhance their understanding of what they have learned. By the end of the course, students should master the basic models and analysis methods of panel data, and be able to skillfully apply these methods to solve problems in their own empirical research. _x000D_

Name: Systems Thinking for Complexity
Introduction:
This course introduces a more comprehensive and systematic way of thinking, called systems thinking. We summarize system thinking as: everything is a system, and all systems are "one yuan, two faces, multi-dimensional and multi-level". It comes from a certain collision and fusion of Eastern traditional Taoist philosophy and quantum mechanics of physics, forming a system that integrates the four levels of "philosophy, science, technology and practice". This course not only introduces theoretical content, but also provides a practical platform for integrating knowledge and action. By forming a practice team with course teaching assistants, students applied the above-mentioned system thinking to solve the following topics closely related to college student life: ① How to continuously improve health; ② How to study efficiently; ③ How to get out of confusion; ④ How to integrate into a team. This course encourages students to rely on this platform to effectively solve the specific difficulties they encounter in actual study and life, and to achieve the improvement of personal quality and life realm. _x000D_

On the one hand, it enriches students' understanding and application of systems thinking, and on the other hand, it stimulates everyone's ambition and feelings through discussions on these topics. Through these discussions, this course aims to inspire everyone to develop a high-level systematic thinking ability during college life, establish a multi-level picture of life, possess the courage and wisdom of an excellent surfer, and lay the foundation for realizing significant life meaning and positive social value in the future information and intelligent era. _x000D_
       To sum up, the purpose of this course is: first, to outline the development and frontiers of systems science, to inspire students to see and have the courage to jump out of the limitations of mechanical thinking, and to expand their learning and scientific research horizons; second, to introduce a new way of thinking - systems thinking, to help students face various problems and situations in study and life. Through the adjustment of thinking and behavior patterns, students can improve their ability to systematically analyze and solve problems, and avoid sub-health states such as entanglement, anxiety, depression, and procrastination; third, guide students to face the problems of human future development, cultivate a big picture, and grow into high-quality talents who integrate Eastern and Western cultures; fourth, inspire students to think about the value of life, thereby gaining the motivation to keep climbing and the source of perseverance. This course will take advantage of the situation to systematically present the life health picture of "wisdom, freedom, and happiness" layer by layer, and encourage students to pursue a happy and valuable life. _x000D_
       Therefore, this course is suitable for all undergraduates (graduate students) who can "open their hearts, put down their dignity, and actively practice" as well as self-learners who have certain knowledge and certain pursuits. _x000D_

Name: Cryptography
Introduction:
Cryptography studies data encryption, digital signatures, message authentication, identification algorithms and protocols. The history of cryptography goes back to ancient times. However, the theory of Shannon, the father of information theory, made cryptography a science. The subsequent proposal of public key cryptography in 1976 was of epoch-making significance. Cryptography is closely related to whether P is equal to NP. Elliptic curves, large number decomposition, lattice theory, Boolean functions, and even quantum mechanics are closely related to cryptography. Computer software and integrated electronic chips have become the carriers of cryptography. Today, passwords are the core in systems such as second-generation ID cards, electronic payments, and electronic signatures. _x000D_
This course guides you into the sacred and profound yet highly applicable field of cryptography.

Name: Foreign Criminal Law
Introduction: Foreign Criminal Law is a general elective course for law majors. This course mainly teaches the criminal law theory of countries with common law systems. The basic content of the course includes, but is not limited to, an introduction to Western criminal law schools, causes and classifications of crimes, legal penalties in British and American criminal law, the definition and origin of criminal law, elements of crime, causation issues in criminal law, criminal intent, legal defense, joint crime, unfinished crimes in British and American criminal law and other important theories. Through the study of this course, students will have a brief understanding of the important contents of foreign criminal law, especially British and American criminal law theory, so as to have a deeper theoretical foundation and reasonable knowledge structure of criminal law, basically master the methods of comparative research, and learn to learn from and apply foreign criminal law theory.

Name: Topics in Market Microstructure Models
Prerequisite: calculus, linear algebra, probability theory, random process
Introduction: This course aims to introduce and explore mathematical, economic and physical models related to market microstructure. Based on the application requirements, the first part of this course will focus on the introduction of stochastic calculus and stochastic control theory. Students who complete the course should have basic knowledge of market microstructure models and their application-related technologies.

Name: Advanced Microeconomics I
Introduction:
This course discusses the basic theories of modern microeconomics, including consumer demand theory, enterprise production theory, etc.
Choice under certain conditions, market structure and pricing, etc. The course content is in-depth based on intermediate microeconomic theory.
ization expansion, emphasizing the rigor of model demonstration, as well as economic intuition and thought. The basic orientation of the course is through learning_x000D_
Classical theory, cultivating economic research capabilities, including understanding the basic norms of economic argumentation and the use of mathematical tools, _x000D_
and the ability to understand and analyze real-life problems with the help of economic theoretical hypotheses.

Name: International Finance
Introduction:
International finance is an economic discipline that studies the monetary aspect of international economic transactions and the inter-temporal allocation of international resources (international lending). In today's highly internationalized and integrated economy and finance, how to keep up with changes in the international financial environment has become one of the central issues that governments and enterprises need to consider when formulating economic policies and business strategies. Therefore, it is very important to master the basic knowledge of international finance and its development. Studying this course will help students understand many economic events occurring internationally and domestically today, such as global economic imbalances, international financial crises, debates on RMB exchange rate policy, etc. _x000D_
_x000D_
This course will introduce the basic theories of international finance and discuss several policy issues: Regarding the basic theories of international finance, we will talk about the balance of payments, the foreign exchange market, the determination of exchange rates, international capital flows, the operation of fixed exchange rate systems and currency crises, etc. Regarding international financial policy issues, we will discuss the international monetary system and its reform, exchange rate system selection, the operation of international financial markets, and several international financial issues in developing countries. _x000D_
_x000D_

Name: Western Humanities in English
College: Department of English Language and Literature
Introduction:
As a course on the history of Western civilization that eliminates Western ideological bias to the greatest extent, "Western Humanities English" cultivates students' English reading and writing skills and critical thinking skills, and strives to enable them to have a more systematic grasp of Western social history and humanistic thoughts while continuously deepening and improving their English language proficiency. The entire course has selected 80 selected articles of 500-600 words from the history of Western culture, covering the history of Western thought and culture from the origin of Mesopotamia, ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, and ancient Rome, through the Renaissance, the Reformation, the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution, and up to the 20th century. Through the systematic construction of Western humanities knowledge and ideas over time, students build a systematic, outline-style Western cultural knowledge system and lay the foundation of history, society and humanistic thoughts for future studies and careers. This course follows the thread of Western humanistic thought, from the origin of human civilization to the culturally diverse society of the 20th century. The basic teaching idea is: take content as the guide, content drives form, and cultural learning drives language learning. Chinese culture is involved in course teaching, which contrasts, collides and echoes with Western culture. In the historical process and cross-cultural exchange activities, it stimulates students' interest, enhances students' understanding and critical awareness of Western thought and culture, and also improves students' ability to spread Chinese culture. The teaching purpose of this course is: This course bases the acquisition of vocabulary and language structures on cultural meanings and humanistic and historical clues, so that they can make sense in a larger cultural context. This course prioritizes meaning generation over language structure, and ideological culture over language form. In this way, students' humanistic knowledge will play a positive role in the acquisition of language forms in the systematic construction, which will have a positive pavement and promotion effect on their future studies. The course teaching takes the history of Western humanistic thought and culture as a vertical line, selects the most representative and influential thinkers and writers, and intercepts chapters of their typical ideological works to form a relatively complete guide to the cultural knowledge system, so that students can have a relatively basic grasp of the overall Western culture while learning English. _x000D_
_x000D_

Name: Geometry Seminar II
Introduction:
In the geometry class of the first semester, we learned about the classification of real conics (and quadratic surfaces) and knew that linear algebra and matrix tools can be used to give very beautiful treatments. In the part of projective geometry, we also know that ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas can be unified, and all non-degenerate quadratic curves are projectively equivalent to each other. Not only that, there are many wonderful things about them, such as: _x000D_
Pascal's theorem, five points determine the quadratic curve. The four points on the quadratic curve can also be used to discuss the cross ratio and harmonic point sequence, and the corresponding poles, _x000D_
The center of a conic can be defined projectively, and even cross ratios can be used to introduce metrics..._x000D_
_x000D_
Going one step further, have you ever thought about the following questions: _x000D_
Can the same method be used to study algebraic curves of third degree or even higher? For example, how to classify? When will the decision be made? Are there any special types that are really good? _x000D_
What is the relationship between the degree (number of generations) of an algebraic curve and its geometric properties? _x000D_
From an algebraic point of view, it is possible to change the number field from real numbers to complex numbers or other finite fields. So is there any difference in conclusion? ……_x000D_
_x000D_
Have you heard of the following? _x000D_
—— There can be "singular points" and "inflection points" on algebraic curves, and generally there are only a limited number of them. They can be defined purely algebraically. _x000D_
——If a curve of degree m and a degree n have no common branches, there will be at most m*n intersection points; if it is a complex algebraic curve and is examined on the complex projective plane, and the intersection points are multiplied, there will be exactly m*n intersection points (Bezout's theorem). _x000D_
——The complex cubic irreducible regular curve can be transformed into the standard form y^2=x(x-1)(x-a). _x000D_
——If two cubic curves without common branches intersect at different 9 points, then any other cubic curve passing through 8 points must pass through the 9th point. This proves Pascal's theorem for quadratic curves. _x000D_
——Addition can be introduced on the point set of cubic curve C to make it a commutative group! The introduction of this algebraic operation has an extremely simple geometric intuition: draw a straight line through two points on C and intersect C at a third point, then define it as the "sum" of the first two points. (If it is a complex cubic irreducible regular curve, then it is actually a torus topologically, and addition can be defined on the torus. This intuition leads us to the field of topology and Riemann surfaces...) _x000D_
——Furthermore, the rational points on the cubic curve are closed to this addition. Moedell's theorem says that this group is a finitely generated commutative group. (We have come to the field of number theory, and the far-reaching development in this area has led to the proof of Fermat's last theorem...) _x000D_
_x000D_
The study of algebraic curves has a long history, dating back to the ancient Greeks who tried to use them to solve three major classical graphing problems. _x000D_
_x000D_
The starting point for learning algebraic curves can be very low, and students as young as freshman can get started and understand it quickly. _x000D_
_x000D_
The connection between algebraic curves is very broad. It uses our mathematical analysis, advanced algebra, geometry (differential geometry), abstract algebra, etc., and stimulates everyone's interest in courses such as number theory/combinatorial, topology, complex variable functions, differential manifolds, and algebraic geometry. _x000D_
_x000D_
The study of algebraic curves can be very deep and cutting-edge. For example, in current studies of structures on four-dimensional manifolds and string theory in physics, algebraic curves (or Riemann surfaces) play a central role in them. _x000D_

Name: Homotopy Theory
Introduction: The basic purpose of this course is to learn some basic core results of homotopy theory and their profound application in differential topology, algebraic geometry, large-scale differential geometry, and large-scale partial differential equations. _x000D_

Name: Calligraphy Aesthetics and Practice
Introduction: The art of calligraphy is the representative of Chinese art. To understand Chinese art, calligraphy is the most convenient way to start. "Calligraphy Aesthetics and Practice" is a cross-department general elective course designed to enable non-calligraphy major students to have a preliminary understanding of the aesthetics of Chinese calligraphy art, a general understanding of the history of Chinese calligraphy, and a basic experience in the basic techniques of Chinese calligraphy. Therefore, this course integrates aesthetics, history and practice. In this course, students not only listen to the history and theory of calligraphy taught by teachers and famous experts, but also practice the five styles of calligraphy themselves: seal script, official script, regular script, running script, and cursive script, inspired by the teacher's unique teaching methods. Students will be improved aesthetically, cultivate their own humanistic and artistic temperament, improve their writing practice, and finally have a new understanding and understanding of Chinese calligraphy art and Chinese artistic spirit.

Name: Selected Topics in Modern Mathematical Physics
Prerequisite: (spring 19-20) It is suggested that there is some knowledge of Lehman's curvature.
Introduction:
In the past 20-30 years, mathematics has undergone profound changes under the influence of modern theoretical physics. The modern mathematical physics produced in this interaction is a new direction in the field of basic mathematics inspired by quantum field theory or string theory. In this course, we will introduce some related topics that have a profound impact on mathematics. _x000D_
_x000D_
The majors in the spring semester of 2019-20 can be topology and geometric recursion. This is a set of recursive relationships defined on the spectral curve by Eynard-Orantin, which comes from the matrix model of physics. Later, Anderson-Borot-Orantin extended this recursion to more abstract geometric recursion relations. These recurrence relations have important implications in counting geometry and mirror symmetry. We will talk about this aspect in detail and give a corresponding introduction to its application.

Name: The Platform Sutra
Introduction: The Tan Sutra is one of the fundamental classics of Zen Buddhism and has also had an important impact on the development of traditional Chinese culture. This course uses the Dunhuang version of the Tan Sutra as the main material, and conducts detailed reading and discussion with reference to various versions popular in later generations to help students deeply understand the basic ideas of Zen and its cultural characteristics. At the same time, it introduces the research methods of religious studies and cultivates the ability to read ancient documents, observe and analyze religious issues.

Name: Gas Dynamics
Introduction: The main contents of this course include: foundation of thermodynamics; basic equations of gas mechanics and its universal integrals, shock waves, Mach waves; characteristic line (surface) method; self-simulating solution, small perturbation method; transonic and hypersonic flow. _x000D_

Name: Computational Fluid Dynamics
Introduction: Computational fluid dynamics is an emerging discipline that uses computers as an important tool to study numerical methods for solving various fluid mechanics problems. The purpose of this course is to introduce some major numerical methods and related basic theoretical knowledge to students by combining typical fluid mechanics problems. Due to the interoperability of numerical methods and their basic theories, their applications are not limited to the field of fluid mechanics. After students learn and master the main content of this course, they will lay a good foundation for their future application and research of numerical methods to solve various physical problems.

Name: New Energy Technology
Prerequisite: General physics, university mathematics, engineering fluids, heat transfer, engineering thermodynamics
Introduction: As a representative technology of energy and resource engineering, new energy technology is crucial to the future development of the national economy and the improvement of people's living standards. This course teaches the basic theory of new energy applications, the structure and principles of new energy conversion devices, and application technologies. On this basis, students can understand the latest developments and trends in new energy technology.

Name: Introduction to Energy and Environmental Engineering
Introduction: Taking the relationship between energy and environment as the main line, the content can be divided into three parts. The first part mainly introduces the classification of energy, the relationship between energy and social and economic development, the resource amount, production and consumption status of traditional energy resources such as coal, oil, natural gas and hydropower resources, and introduces the resource status and status of new energy sources such as nuclear energy, solar energy, geothermal energy, wind energy, ocean energy, tidal energy, biomass energy, hydrogen energy and natural gas hydrates. Development and utilization of technologies; the second part focuses on the basic knowledge of environmental science, discusses the environmental pollution control issues caused by the energy conversion and utilization process, and introduces pollution prevention and control technologies in detail; the third part is a team of teachers from the Department of Energy introducing various cutting-edge research work being carried out in the department to help students understand the research status of the department.

Name: Cycling
Prerequisite: No, you can choose classes on bicycles.
Introduction: The cycling education course takes a broader "education" perspective and is divided into three themes to educate Peking University undergraduates on "people and vehicles education, environment and travel education, nature and society", and promotes healthy lifestyles and green travel. The teaching method of the course is characterized by the "3Ps", namely professors' presentation (Professors Presentation), students' discussion presentation (students' presentation), and students' vehicle setup, maintenance and riding practice (Practice). _x000D_

Name: Introduction to Biomechanics and Medical Engineering
Introduction: Biomechanics and medical engineering are emerging forces in the development of medicine and biology today. They are the new driving force and growth point for the development of modern mechanics disciplines. They cover multiple disciplines such as biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, materials, mechanics and engineering. Its basic task is to use mechanics (engineering) technical means to research and solve related problems in biology and medicine. Biomechanics and medical engineering play an important role in ensuring human health and providing disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation services, and have become an important foundation and pillar of the current medical and health industry. This course will introduce the basic concepts, main technical methods and typical applications of biomechanics and medical engineering, stimulate students' interest in biomechanics and medical engineering, and lay the foundation for in-depth study of related courses in the future.

Name: Modern Manufacturing Technology and Practice
Introduction: Modern machining technology includes theory, practice and discussion. 1. The theoretical content of the course is a series of new process methods such as EDM forming and piercing processing, wire EDM processing, electrochemical processing, laser processing, ultrasonic processing, electron beam and ion beam processing, rapid prototyping, water jet cutting and plasma arc cutting. 2. The practical content of the course is combined with small project production to familiarize students with the technical and cultural connotations of modern processing technology; 3. The discussion content of the course allows students to participate in teacher-led classroom discussions, thereby exercising students' practical and innovative abilities.

Name: Theoretical Mechanics
Prerequisite: calculus, linear algebra and geometry, constant differential equation, general physics
Introduction: The basic knowledge of theoretical mechanics is widely used in engineering practice, such as static analysis, motion analysis and dynamic analysis. Theoretical mechanics is the main prerequisite course in mechanics major courses. Its basic concepts, basic theories and basic methods are the necessary foundation for a series of subsequent professional courses. Theoretical mechanics teaching is of great significance to the training of students' thinking methods, the improvement of analysis and problem-solving abilities, and the cultivation of comprehensive quality.

Name: Metalworking Practicum
Introduction: This course has a total of 60 hours and 3 credits, and students can complete it during the summer. Teacher teaching and factory internship are conducted at the same time, with teacher teaching accounting for 22 credit hours and factory internship accounting for 38 credit hours. It mainly cultivates students’ basic skills in metal processing and mechanical operation. Through metalworking internship, students can understand the basic knowledge and procedures of experimental safety, process technology and industrial machinery operation. The course is divided into ten chapters, including practical content such as casting, welding, steel heat treatment, basic knowledge of cutting processing, turning, milling, planing, grinding, benchwork, CNC machining technology, etc.

Name: Engine Combustion
Introduction:
Engine combustion is an important course for the aerospace undergraduate major in the School of Engineering. It is an important professional course for my country's aerospace propulsion theory and engineering, power engineering, and engineering thermophysics. However, my country's aviation colleges generally only offer aerospace engine combustion courses, and aerospace colleges only offer rocket engine courses. According to the curriculum design requirements of the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, aviation and aerospace engine combustion needs to be set as a course, including aerospace engine combustion, rocket engine combustion and new concept engine combustion. _x000D_
This course is a highly engineering professional course with rich and extensive content. While emphasizing the basic theory of combustion, it also focuses on the combustion practice of engine engineering. The main task of this course is to enable students to master the basic theories and methods of combustion, master the combustion process and combustion working principles in aerospace engines, ramjet engines, pulse detonation engines and rocket engines, and lay the foundation for students to engage in various aerospace engine research, combustion chamber design and related combustion research. _x000D_
Chapter 1 is the introduction. Aerospace propulsion principles, development, structural characteristics, working processes, thermodynamic cycles, and main indicators of various types of engines, including: (1) aerospace engines: piston engines, turbojet engines, turbofan engines, turboprop engines, and turboshaft engines; (2) ramjet engines; (3) pulse detonation engines; (4) rocket engines. _x000D_
Chapter 2 covers the basic theory of combustion. Including: (1) Combustion reaction kinetics, basic knowledge of combustion chemical kinetics, reaction rate, chain reaction, law of mass action, Arrhenius law, divided collision theory, etc., and factors affecting chemical reactions; (2) Ignition and flameout, basic concepts and mechanisms of ignition (thermal natural theory) and flameout, ignition mechanism and model; (3) Flame propagation and stability, laminar flame, turbulent flame Concepts and propagation mechanisms and influencing factors, flame stabilization mechanisms and flame stabilization theory in high-speed airflow; (4) Fuel atomization and nozzles, liquid fuel atomization mechanisms and influencing factors, structures and parameters of straight-flow nozzles, centrifugal nozzles, pneumatic nozzles, evaporation tube nozzles, oil throw plate nozzles, etc.; (5) Liquid fuel combustion, basic theories of liquid fuel evaporation and gas-liquid two-phase combustion, oil droplet evaporation and combustion models. _x000D_
    Chapter 3 covers the main combustion chamber of aeroengines. Including (1) Overview of the main combustion chamber, combustion chamber functions, working characteristics, performance parameters, structural types, and working processes; (2) Characteristics and performance of each component of the main combustion chamber, including combustion chamber air flow distribution, diffuser, swirler, fuel nozzle, flame tube, ignition, and combustion chamber cooling; (3) Mass balance and energy balance during the combustion process of the main combustion chamber, and calculation of thermal parameters; (4) Production mechanism of combustion pollutants, low-pollution combustion chamber. _x000D_
Chapter 4 covers the aero-engine afterburner. Including (1) working characteristics, performance parameters, working process and impact on the engine of the afterburner; (2) performance characteristics of turbojet and turbofan engines and comparison of afterburners; (3) characteristics and performance of various components of the afterburner, including mixer, flame stabilizer type and layout, nozzle and layout, and ignition method; (4) low-pressure combustion in the afterburner; (5) oscillating combustion in the afterburner. _x000D_
    Chapter 5 covers ramjet combustion. Including (1) ramjet engine development structure type, characteristics and performance; (2) combustion organization principles, including subsonic and supersonic combustion technology characteristics, liquid fuel combustion organization principles, solid fuel organization combustion principles; (3) liquid and solid ramjet engine combustion chamber design; (4) supersonic combustion chamber working characteristics and combustion organization; (5) dual-mode combustion chamber principle and design. _x000D_
Chapter 6 covers pulse detonation and pulsation engine combustion. Including (1) the formation, propagation and characteristics of detonation and pulsation combustion; (2) pulse detonation and pulsation combustion organization; (3) key technologies of pulse detonation and pulsation engines; (4) pulse detonation engines controlled by rotary valves; (5) air-breathing two-phase pulse detonation engines. _x000D_
Chapter 7 covers rocket engine combustion. Including (1) rocket engine overview and performance indicators; (2) solid rocket engine combustion process; (3) liquid rocket engine combustion process; (4) rocket engine combustion chamber design principles. _x000D_

This course is a supplement to Methods of Mathematical Physics (Part 2) and is started at the same time as Methods of Mathematical Physics (Part 2). Arrange teaching assistants to give lectures as needed. _x000D_
Methods of Mathematical Physics (Part 2) is a course with a lot of content, few hours of study, and high difficulty. At the same time, the course is very important and is the basis for subsequent physics courses. It is very necessary to arrange special exercise classes, and only one study hour per week is enough. Considering that Mathematical Physics Methods (Part 2) is a three-credit class and only takes one class every two weeks, it is recommended that this class be arranged in two weeks for two class hours.
Introduction: Mathematical physics methods exercise course is a supplement to mathematical physics methods course. According to the students' homework situation, the exercises and assignments are properly explained. It is hoped that through this method, students can have a better grasp of relevant knowledge.

Name: Mesopotamian Art and Civilization (Foundations of Civilization)
Introduction: Based on the general background of the development history of world civilization, this course guides students to understand the unique visual and material culture of ancient Mesopotamia, the "cradle of human civilization", through the explanation and investigation of the origin, development, style characteristics and historical changes of art and architecture in ancient Mesopotamia (Mesopotamia). The course strives to break through the vision of civilization under the framework of the traditional Western "Orientalism" and uses Chinese civilization as the ontology and potential comparison object. It guides students to think about the common problems faced by human civilization during the rise and fall of Mesopotamian civilization, and enhances the awareness and ability of civilized dialogue in the context of globalization. At the methodological level, the course is committed to introducing some basic research paths in the art history discipline into the teaching, that is, starting from visual materials, combining documentary records and archaeological materials, and exploring the unique civilizational forms and cultural traditions behind them through the viewing, interpretation and interpretation of "pictures" and "objects".

Name: Basic Principles of Aircraft Engines
Introduction: This course is a professional course with a strong engineering focus. It covers a wide range of content and explains the basic principles and structures of various types of engines. The main task is to enable students to understand the basic theories, methods, and principles of internal flow in engines, and to lay a foundation for students to engage in research on various types of aerospace engines. The main content includes basic theory, turbojet and turbofan engines, inlets, compressors, turbines, main combustion chambers, afterburners, exhaust devices, turboprop engines, turboshaft engines, ramjet engines, detonation engines, and rocket engines.

Name: English for Specific Purposes
Introduction: This course is designed for undergraduate students majoring in science and mechanics to further improve their English listening, speaking, writing and reading skills in combination with their majors after learning college English. The content includes introducing basic mechanical concepts, formulas and methods in English, and reading basic English selections in engineering sciences such as theoretical mechanics, material mechanics, elastic-plastic mechanics, fluid mechanics, biomechanics, mechanical experiments, computational simulation and applications.

Name: Energy and Propulsion
Introduction: This course will introduce the basic knowledge of thermodynamics and combustion involved in internal combustion engines, gas turbines and thrusters, focus on the process of converting fossil fuel chemical energy into thermal energy, and analyze the flow and combustion phenomena involved, so that students can master the basic thermodynamics and combustion knowledge involved in energy conversion and propulsion technology.

Name: Religious Art and Religious Belief
Prerequisite: “Initiative of Religious Science” or courses on the major religions of the world, etc.
Introduction: The course covers a wide range of artistic aspects of the early religions of Christianity, Orthodoxism, Islam, Buddhism and Taoism in the world, including, in particular, the aesthetics of ancient Christian religions, Orthodox iconic arts, Islamic architecture and decorations, Buddhist pagoda temples and mural art, and the memorizations in Taoism and the religious beliefs in ancient Chinese mountains.

Name: Fundamentals of Materials Science (Part 1)
Introduction:
Fundamentals of Materials Science is an important basic course for the major of Materials Science and Engineering, involving materials physics, physical chemistry, materials thermodynamics and other disciplines. Through the teaching of this course, students can master the basic knowledge in the field of materials science and the basic experimental skills of materials experiments. _x000D_
    The course uses "Fundamentals of Materials Science" edited by Professor Yu Yongning (2006 edition of Higher Education Press) as the main reference textbook, combined with relevant domestic and foreign textbooks. The teaching content focuses on the basic concepts and basic theories of materials science, and displays the latest research results in related fields. It will be based on the theory of metallic materials, integrate the content of inorganic non-metallic materials and polymer materials, and highlight the common characteristics of materials. Focusing on the relationship between the chemical composition, organizational structure, processing technology and performance of materials and their changing rules, this article systematically introduces the material structure, crystal defects, crystallization and solidification, phase structure and phase diagram, interface, diffusion in solids, material thermodynamics, plastic deformation and recrystallization, phase changes in materials, etc. and their interrelationships. For teaching content with strong conceptual and abstract content, such as crystal structure, crystal defects, plastic deformation, phase diagrams, etc., the advantages of multimedia teaching are fully utilized, and methods such as images and three-dimensional animation are used to enhance the teaching effect. _x000D_
    During the teaching process, students are also organized to visit the college's characteristic laboratories to enable students to understand the characteristics of the materials discipline and cultivate professional interests. _x000D_

Name: Laboratory Safety and Protection
Introduction: This course will systematically introduce common laboratory safety accidents and prevention methods, including physical and chemical unsafe factors, handling of hazardous chemicals, microbial and biochemical material safety, fire safety, safety precautions in the workplace, personal protection measures, accident scene handling and first aid methods, etc.

Name: Analytical Chemistry
Introduction: Analytical chemistry course is one of the main basic courses for students majoring in materials and chemistry. Its theories and methods are not only the basis of analytical chemistry, but also the basis for work in chemical education, chemistry, biology, geology, environment and other disciplines. The analytical chemistry class not only teaches students the basic principles and methods of analytical chemistry, but also enables students to establish a strict concept of "quantity". Through the study of this course, students can master the basic principles of analytical chemistry and chemical quantitative analysis methods, master each step in the quantitative analysis process, learn the sources of errors in analysis and determination, the representation of errors, and initially learn the statistical processing methods of experimental data, understand the principles and applications of separation methods commonly used in chemical analysis, and have the ability to solve common analytical chemistry problems and the skills to independently conduct chemical analysis experiments.

Name: Physical Chemistry
Introduction: Introduction to Physical Chemistry teaches basic knowledge of physical chemistry to undergraduates in engineering departments. The book includes ten chapters: the first law of thermodynamics, the second law of thermodynamics, chemical potential, chemical equilibrium, multiphase equilibrium, preliminary statistical thermodynamics, electrochemistry, surface phenomena and dispersed systems, basic principles of chemical kinetics, and composite reaction kinetics.

Name: Fundamentals of Materials Science (Part 2)
Introduction: The material science base is an important basic course in material science and engineering, covering the disciplines of material physics, physical chemistry and thermal sciences of materials.

Name: English for Materials Science and Engineering
Introduction: Teach the basic structure, physical processes, properties, and potential applications of various materials. Including the atomic and molecular structure and chemical bonds of materials; metal and ceramic materials; organic materials; defects, deformation, reinforcement and destruction mechanisms of solid materials; phase diagrams and phase change processes; mechanical properties of materials; composite materials; electrical properties of materials; nanomaterials and electronic devices; application prospects of materials in various fields, etc.

Name: Engineering Literature Retrieval and Technical Writing
Introduction:
Information and writing literacy are the basic needs for cultivating talents' innovative abilities and are also the basis for learning and research. This course cultivates students' information and writing qualities, enhances students' information awareness, and masters the skills of acquiring, utilizing, and developing engineering literature information resources; it enables students to understand the writing knowledge and skills of various scientific and technological genres, and master writing theories, writing methods, and writing skills. It has important and far-reaching significance for promoting students to continuously absorb new knowledge, improve knowledge structure, improve self-learning ability, scientific research ability, adaptability, and scientific writing ability, give full play to their creative talents, implement comprehensive quality education, and apply what they have learned. _x000D_
_x000D_
This course uses a teaching method that combines multimedia teaching with real-time online demonstrations. It will focus on engineering literature information resources, literature classification and subject analysis; literature retrieval technology; search engine retrieval functions, retrieval of Chinese engineering literature databases (such as Tsinghua Tongfang Academic Journal Network, VIP Database, Wanfang Database, etc.), foreign literature databases (such as Engineering Index EI, Science Abstracts, Science Citation Index SCI, Chemical Abstracts CA, etc.), patent information, dissertations, standard information, etc.; retrieval and comprehensive utilization of network information resources. Through learning, students are required to flexibly master the methods and techniques of network information retrieval, including selecting databases, formulating search strategies, and analyzing search results; they can independently use network search engines and network database searches according to the search topic, and quickly and accurately retrieve the required information through multiple channels; master the methods of obtaining original documents, and cultivate the ability to integrate and publish information. _x000D_
_x000D_
This course focuses on the close integration of basic theory and practical application, with scientific research and ability development as its guiding ideology. It will focus on teaching the basic theories, types, characteristics, writing methods and writing skills of scientific writing. Following the basic knowledge of writing and commonly used stylistic writing ideas, it briefly introduces the basic theoretical knowledge of scientific and technological writing, focusing on experimental and theoretical papers, literature reviews and review papers; graduation projects, dissertation proposal reports, dissertations; experimental (internship) reports, science and technology reports; scientific and technological achievement applications, science fund project applications; invention patent specifications; showing students some famous works, and finally introduces the methods and strategies for submitting journal papers and domestic and foreign academic conference papers. _x000D_

Name: Nanomaterials Science and Technology
Prerequisite: Solid physics, material science base, general physics, etc.
Introduction: This course mainly teaches the basic concepts and connotations of nanoscience and nanotechnology, as well as related physical foundations, hot topics such as preparation methods, characterization methods, basic structures, physical and chemical properties of nanomaterials and nanostructures, and their potential applications.

Name: Materials Chemistry
Introduction: This course is a professional basic course for undergraduate students in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering. It is also an elective course for undergraduate students in other majors in the School of Engineering and graduate students in various majors. Through the study of this course, students are expected to master the basic knowledge and principles of materials chemistry, understand the development status of materials chemistry, and lay the foundation for students to engage in scientific research in materials science in the future. The course includes four parts: basics of materials chemistry, principles and methods of material chemistry preparation, functional materials chemistry, and applications of materials chemistry in several types of new materials research fields. The first part introduces the subject foundation of materials chemistry from the foundation of materials science, chemistry foundation and crystallography foundation, so that students can selectively improve the basic knowledge required for this course according to their own situation, and at the same time guide students on how to learn materials chemistry. The second part focuses on the chemical synthesis and preparation principles of materials from solid phase, liquid phase and gas phase chemical synthesis methods. The third part takes several types of functional materials as examples to reveal the relationship between the composition, chemical preparation and processing of materials and the structure and properties of materials. The fourth part introduces the application of materials chemistry in the design and preparation of new materials with examples. During the teaching process, try to introduce the latest developments in materials chemistry to cultivate students' interest in learning this course.

Name: Materials Science and Engineering Laboratory
Introduction: The materials science and engineering experimental course is a basic experimental course for materials majors. The experimental content is oriented towards new materials and new technologies, and strives to reflect the characteristics of the combination of materials science and engineering. It covers various aspects such as metallic materials, functional ceramic materials, semiconductor materials, polymer materials, nanomaterials and devices, and material characterization. The course focuses on cultivating the hands-on ability of undergraduates, and combines the development trends of materials disciplines with the department’s key research directions such as nanomaterials and micro-nano devices, new energy materials and devices, biomedical materials and devices, organic polymers and composite materials, and designs eight basic teaching experiments including observation of microscopic morphology of materials, quantitative analysis of chemical elements, and preparation and testing of nanomaterials.

Name: Semiconductor Physics and Devices
Introduction:
Semiconductor physics and devices are the foundation of modern electronic technology and engineering. This course mainly introduces the basic knowledge of modern semiconductor physics and electronic devices, including basic theoretical knowledge of semiconductor physics, basic working principles of semiconductor electronic devices, some important physical effects and electronic applications. At the same time, this course also uses a small number of chapters to introduce emerging nanoelectronic devices, and electronic devices with certain functions (such as sensing). The course is divided into four parts with a total of 13 chapters: the first part is an introductory chapter that provides an overview of semiconductors and modern integrated electronics, including emerging nano-semiconductor electronic devices; the second part is a basic chapter (chapters 1-6) to learn the basic physical knowledge of semiconductor devices, mainly including crystal structure, preliminary knowledge of quantum mechanics and theory, semiconductor energy band theory, and equilibrium and non-equilibrium carriers in semiconductors. , carrier transport phenomena and transport equations, etc., laying a good foundation for the study of semiconductor devices; the third part of semiconductor devices (Chapter 7-13), learning semiconductor p-n junction and metal-semiconductor heterojunction diodes, field effect transistors, bipolar junction transistors, optoelectronic devices, etc., as well as related basic physical effects, device working principles and theoretical analysis. The fourth part, Emerging Devices (Chapter 13), introduces the recently developed nanoelectronics and other non-semiconductor functional electronic devices, such as graphene, carbon nanotube nanoelectronic devices, ferroelectric, piezoelectric, magnetoelectric and magnetoresistive electronic devices, etc. _x000D_
This course is suitable for teaching senior undergraduate students majoring in science and engineering. The learning targets include senior undergraduate students majoring in materials or engineering mechanics, electronics and information, physics, and instrumentation. _x000D_

Name: Analysis and Testing of Material Properties
Introduction: This course will introduce the basic knowledge and cutting-edge applications in the field of material performance analysis and testing, including material device optical analysis and testing, material device electrical analysis and testing, material surface performance analysis and testing, etc.

Name: Polymer Materials Science and Engineering
Introduction: The main goal of this course is to try to enable learners to comprehensively understand and understand polymer materials from the perspectives of chemistry, physics and materials. First, the polymerization process and methods from monomers to polymers are introduced, including stepwise polymerization, free radical polymerization, ionic polymerization, coordination polymerization, etc. Secondly, the characteristics of polymers are introduced from a physical perspective, such as polymer chain structure, aggregate structure, mechanical and electrical properties and other properties. Then, production methods such as polymer blending modification and molding processing are introduced. On this basis, some of the latest functional polymer materials are introduced, such as conductive polymers, liquid crystal polymers, photosensitive polymers, etc.

Name: Inorganic Non-Metallic Materials Science and Engineering
Introduction: This course introduces the basic theoretical knowledge of the common properties of inorganic non-metallic materials, as well as the core knowledge units and knowledge points in the field of material preparation in professional specifications. Including material preparation and processing methods and principles; the structure, properties, and preparation processes of traditional materials such as oxides, carbides, nitrides, glass, ceramics, cement, and concrete; knowledge of the preparation of low-dimensional materials such as powders and films, etc. At the same time, combined with the development status of new materials, a moderate introduction to new materials, new theories, new scientific research progress and trends is given, especially the new carbon nanomaterials with application prospects that have emerged in recent years, such as carbon nanotubes and graphene. The course will introduce the synthesis technology, structural characteristics, physical and chemical properties of these new materials, as well as their application research in electronic devices, new energy, environment and other fields. Through the study of this course, students can master the preparation principles and production processes of inorganic non-metallic materials, as well as the commonalities and characteristics of technological processes, so that students can have a comprehensive understanding of the properties, production processes and applications of inorganic non-metallic materials, and at the same time establish basic concepts of new materials, new processes and new methods.

Name: Metallic Materials Science and Engineering
Introduction: Metal materials are the most commonly used materials among all materials, and their theories and systems are relatively complete. This course formulates the teaching content in accordance with the "Metal Materials" course syllabus for undergraduate majors in materials science and engineering, metal materials engineering and metallurgical engineering in colleges and universities. It focuses on the knowledge of the basic principles of metal materials and teaches basic knowledge related to steel materials, non-ferrous metal materials, metal functional materials, new metal materials and metal material forming technology. The course will systematically introduce the alloying principles of steel materials, including the interaction between alloying elements and iron and carbon, the role of alloying elements in various phase transformation processes, their impact on material strengthening and toughening, and the characteristics of alloy steel process performance. At the same time, focusing on the main line of material composition - process - organization - performance - application, the course will introduce common steel materials such as various types of machine parts steel, tool and mold steel, special performance steel, cast iron, and typical non-ferrous metal alloy materials such as aluminum, copper, titanium, and magnesium. Based on the development of materials, some relatively mature new metal materials will be introduced, such as magnetic alloys, metal matrix composite materials, micro-alloy non-quenched and tempered steel, environmentally compatible metal materials (such as simple alloys, general alloys), etc. Finally, some typical metal material forming technologies will be introduced, including solidification, plastic forming and welding.

Name: Introduction to Materials Physics
Introduction: It mainly explains the physical aspects of materials science, so that students can have a comprehensive study and understanding of basic physical issues in the field of materials science, and lay a physical foundation for the next step of scientific research and practical work. The content mainly includes mechanical issues of materials, focusing on the basis of quantum mechanics of materials; thermal issues of materials, including an overview of thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, the three laws of thermodynamics, heat capacity of materials, thermal expansion and heat conduction and other basic concepts; electrical issues of materials, focusing on metal free electron theory, energy band theory, dielectric properties of materials, etc.; magnetic and optical properties of materials, etc. Finally, we briefly introduce the function conversion problem of materials.

Name: Fundamentals of Quantum Mechanics for Materials Science
Introduction:
Quantum mechanics is the basic theory for studying the laws of motion of microscopic particles. Together with the theory of relativity, it constitutes the two basic pillars of modern physics. Many physical theories and sciences are based on quantum mechanics; it is widely used in materials science, energy science, optoelectronic technology, biomedical engineering and other disciplines. This course is an elective course for undergraduates in the School of Engineering. It aims to provide the necessary theoretical foundation for subsequent courses and improve students' ability to analyze and solve problems. _x000D_
_x000D_
    This course will focus on the wave-particle duality of particles, the statistical interpretation of wave functions, the state superposition principle, the Schrödinger equation, the relationship between operators and mechanical quantities, the commutation relationship and uncertainty relationship of operators, the matrix representation of operators, positive transformation, Dirac symbol, spin and spin function of electrons, identical particles and the principle of identity, etc. Basic concepts and principles. Through the teaching of this course: 1) enable students to understand the movement laws of microscopic particles, Preliminarily master the basic concepts and principles of quantum mechanics and basic methods for dealing with typical problems, thereby enhancing the understanding of the microscopic world; 2) Understand the impact and regulation of quantum effects on the physical properties of materials, thereby deepening the understanding and understanding of new materials and their strange properties; 3) Cultivate new ways of thinking from a quantum perspective, and improve the ability to analyze and solve problems; 4) Understand the wide application of quantum mechanics in materials science, energy science, and optoelectronic technology, laying the foundation for further learning and scientific research in the future. _x000D_
_x000D_

Name: Ancient Chinese History (Part 2)
Introduction: This course is for undergraduates who are not majoring in history. It takes the general trend of the evolution of political history and institutional history in the second half of ancient China (960-1840) as the main clue, so that students can have a clearer framework for the development of ancient Chinese history. It guides students to strengthen their reading after class, hoping to enhance students' interest in ancient Chinese history and stimulate students' thinking.

Name: Frontier Issues in China's Public Finance
Introduction: This course covers cutting-edge issues in China's finance, including the scale and structure of government revenue and expenditure and their existing problems, existing problems and reform directions of China's tax system, public infrastructure construction and the provision of public goods, social security systems for urban employees, public institutions, and farmers, medical security system reform, central and local government debt, fiscal policy and China's economic growth, central and local financial rights and powers and central and local fiscal transfer payments, the establishment of new tax categories for local governments, traditional Chinese fiscal and taxation ideas and their impact on contemporary finance, etc. This course aims to enable students to deeply understand the current situation and existing problems of China's finance, understand the commonalities and characteristics of China's finance and that of other countries, and use basic economic theories and methods to observe and analyze contemporary China's fiscal issues. _x000D_

Name: Structural Mechanics and Matrix Methods
Prerequisite: Higher mathematics, theoretical mechanics, material mechanics
Introduction: Structural mechanics and its matrix method is one of the important professional basic courses (main basic courses) for the engineering structural analysis major. It is a required course for the engineering structural analysis major and a restricted course for the theoretical and applied mechanics major.

Name: Industrial Organization
Introduction: Industrial organization theory studies corporate behavior in different market environments, including pricing theory, games between companies, the impact of corporate behavior on social welfare and consumer welfare, and the role of government or industry organizations in the market. Industrial organization belongs to the enterprise theory part of microeconomics and occupies an important position in the economic theory system with market mechanism as the core. Among them, the discussion of market efficiency is of significant significance to the design of economic systems. Industrial organization theory has been widely used in understanding corporate behavior, guiding antitrust practice, and improving government regulations. This course mainly involves the basic theory of industrial organization.

Name: Socioeconomic Survey Data Analysis
Prerequisite: Theoretical methods and practices of socio-economic surveys or participation in the Summer Survey of Healthy Ageings in China
Introduction:
This course is for interviewers who have completed the China Health and Retirement Tracking Survey. Through training courses and field surveys, students have become familiar with the process of survey data collection and obtained first-hand information about how people live, work, and interact with their families and society. This course will teach students how to use this data to conduct research and write research papers. Specifically, students will learn how to use Stata statistical software to process data, how to create descriptive statistical tables, how to conduct more complex statistical analysis, and how to use data to write research papers. _x000D_
_x000D_
This course will be divided into four parts of roughly equal length. The first part teaches the use of statistical software, allowing students to perform basic operations on survey data and create descriptive statistical tables. The second part teaches statistical knowledge so that students can understand how to use survey data to conduct more in-depth regression analysis and how to interpret the regression results. Part Three teaches and practices methods for writing research papers using survey data. The fourth part is to provide concentrated thematic guidance on students’ thesis topic selection. _x000D_
_x000D_
The first three parts of the teaching content, namely data manipulation and statistical description table production, regression analysis and paper writing skills, are mainly taught by faculty, supplemented by classroom tutoring and extracurricular exercises. The fourth part, namely research guidance, is mainly based on student reports, supplemented by faculty comments and guidance on students' research design. The student's thesis report will be controlled to less than one quarter. Faculty will grade all assignments and provide feedback on papers. _x000D_
_x000D_
The first half of the class will be assigned weekly assignments, there will be a short paper requirement in the middle of the semester, and a complete research paper will be submitted at the end of the semester. The grade ratio is: 30% homework, 30% short paper, and 40% final paper. _x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
