Name: Francophone World Literature
Introduction:
The course will provide an overview of the cultural origin and literature of the French-speaking regions of the world in the context of French history, will examine important works of writers from the French-speaking region of Africa and the French overseas departments, and will analyse their content and their literary achievements from a multi-dimensional perspective of intercultural anthropology, post-colonial theory, poetry, cultural research and linguistics.
Students need basic knowledge of Western history and literature, preliminary knowledge of Western modern thinking and literature theory in the twentieth century, and a reading base in English or French. Through this course, students are asked to become aware of important writers and works of the world's French literature, to get an overview of current French literature, including in Black Africa and the Caribbean, to deepen their problem-aware consciousness, to take an intercultural view of the current literary ecology of the world, to learn some critical words, including cultural research, structuralistic text analysis, and ultimately to reflect on the worldwide development of indigenous literature.

Name: Doctoral Thesis Writing and Research (I)
Introduction: Seminars are organized on a weekly or weekly basis by students on the relevant content of their paper and on important references, and research reports are presented and discussed by the lead teacher with all students. The chair teacher chooses critical literature and theoretical writings of reference value for doctoral thesis research, requiring students to prepare for reading in advance and to conduct classroom discussions or post-school reports. Classroom discussions are conducted under the auspices of teachers, who may also designate relevant works and critical literature on the basis of their own reading lists.

Name: Historical Representation in Contemporary Western Fiction
Introduction: After almost a century of silence, the traditional historical novels created by Scott were revived in a new form in the contemporary era, re-examining the relationship between history and novels, history and history, memories and texts, historical narratives and ideologies, official history and private history in a new historical perspective, reflecting a rethinking of history and traditions by writers in a modern wave. The objective of this course is to explore how they represent historical time and space and the historical consciousness of writers by reading presentations by representatives of representative contemporary writers, Bolhess, Von Negut, Pinchin, Kufuor, Doktoro and Reed. In addition to a specific text analysis of novels, the course will theoretically trace Nietzsche and Foco's spectrographs, Benjamin's "reverse combing history", Hayden White's "won history" and the "cultural poetry" of New History, with a view to raising the analysis of the form and content of these novels to theoretical levels.

Name: Graduate First Foreign Language: Japanese
Introduction: The course is a compulsory course in foreign languages for highly developed graduate students with Japanese as their first foreign language.

Name: Theory and Critical Methods of the Novel
The Modern Convergence of Chinese and Western Thought
Victorian Cultural Criticism and Social Thought
Introduction: The purpose of this course is to present cultural criticism and social thinking during the Victorian period in the United Kingdom. During this period of unprecedented social criticism in the United Kingdom, discussions about “culture” were intense, and many ideas were significant and far-reaching for future generations. In the study of English and American literature of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Victorian social thought is not only a key background, but also a significant part of the text itself is an excellent subject of literary research. In terms of content selection, this course focuses mainly on the concept of essays (non-fiction prose) and includes a certain amount of novels and poetry. The curriculum structure will run along the main lines and sidelines: the main lines, which are the social critics and works of the United Kingdom that have far-reaching implications for future generations during this period, such as Thomas Carlyle, On Liberty of John Stuart Mill, Culture and Anarchy of Matthew Arnold, Adam Bede of George Eliot and John Ruskin, and Stones of Venice, among others; and other authors and their works that have raised concerns or caused controversy in the area of social criticism during this period, such as Herbert Spencer, Samuel Smiles, James Phillips Kay-Shuttleworth and others. On the one hand, the curriculum will lead students to read the content of the main lines, dig into the content of some important ideas (ideas) in the classic texts of social criticism, and give the necessary attention to the expression of these social criticisms (i.e. “voice” and “style”); On the other hand, the curriculum will encourage students to expand their reading skills by linking sideline content to the content of the main line, and by comparing and reflecting on how people reconcile and disagree, in terms of perception and expression, in order to achieve a more comprehensive understanding and in-depth reflection of the social criticisms of Victorian society.

Name: Consumer Culture: History and Theory
Introduction: The course covers three areas: the history of consumer culture in Western origin and development; the basic concepts of Western consumer culture theory; and aesthetic, sociological and psychological analysis of contemporary consumer cultural phenomena. Consumerism is a socio-cultural phenomenon that has emerged with the emergence of modernity in the West, with its early limitation to the noble class. By the second half of the nineteenth century, the culture of consumption had evolved rapidly among the middle class and among the civil population, and today it has become an integral part of our daily lives. This course, which began in the eighteenth century in Britain, traces the origins and development of consumer societies in the West and describes how consumerism has been globalized from Europe to the rest of the world. The consumption of goods is not only a material activity, it is accompanied by the ideology of spiritual activity, such as aesthetics and art, and is closely related to the cultural identity of human beings. This has made possible aesthetic and cultural analysis of commodity consumption. A study of the culture of consumption can better illustrate how goods and consumption manipulate human aesthetics and everyday patterns. Understanding the impact of consumer culture on human society helps us to understand the development of contemporary aesthetic culture. Contemporary cultural criticism provides us with the theoretical tools to take a fresh look at the development and spread of consumer culture in the context of capital expansion and aestheticization worldwide. The course will present a wealth of historical and realistic textual and photographic material illustrating the full extent of capital penetration of human behaviour, emotions and aesthetic senses in the consumer culture. The course covered the works of Marx, Van Buren, Zimel, Lukachi, Adono, Malcusa, Balt, Debo, Bodira, Desedo, Budieu, Haug, Williams, Jaminsin and leading scholars of contemporary consumer cultural theory, Colin Campbell, Mike Featherstone, John Fiske and others, and addressed and applied important concepts of consumer cultural theory, such as: Modernity, self (self), body, space, materialization, aestheticization, lifestyle, cultural industry, identity, image, class, etc. ended with an analysis of consumerism in English and American literature at the end of the nineteenth century. The purpose of the course is three-fold: first, to have a clear understanding of the history and current state of development of the consumer culture of Western capitalism. ii. To form a critical position and view of the various consumer cultural phenomena based on reading and understanding the theory of the consumer culture, different from popular thinking and thinking. III. Theoretical analytical methods and tools for contemporary cultural criticism. The requirements for students to be selected: there is a literary, aesthetic and cultural theoretical foundation; there is thought and confusion about the fate of literature and aesthetics in contemporary society; there is interest in the philosophical, aesthetic and cultural significance of commodity consumption.

Name: Chinese and Western Translation Traditions
Introduction: The course focuses on the history of translation between China and the major Western countries (including near-modern Japan) from ancient times to the present, helps students to organize important translation events and representative translators and translations over various historical periods and to understand the trajectory of translation changes; and interprets the main features of translation activity in different historical periods and in different cultural contexts, based on the basic familiarity of students with the history of Chinese and Western translation, with a particular emphasis on the interaction of translation in different cultural contexts with a global awareness of globalization, with a focus on analysing the interaction of translation with political, religious, power, literature, popular culture, ideology and social change in general, as well as the development of the theory of translation, thereby helping students to understand the diverse translation traditions. In doing so, an attempt will be made to recognize translation traditions from a variety of perspectives, including cultural research, deconstructionism, post-colonial criticism and feminism, based on the use of traditional history and translation theories, with the aim of developing students ' perspectives and capacity to understand and analyse problems.

Name: The Ancient Western Epic Tradition
Introduction: This course focuses on the origins, development and implications for future generations of the ancient Western epics, focusing on the homage of the homage (Ilyat, Odyssey) and Virgil's epics (Igned) ... The focus of the course was on the classical epics in the legal, the rhetorical, and the basic features of the literature, the centrality of the epics in ancient education, the close relationship between the epics and the ancients of the academic (school surveying, ailmentation, solvenia). We will also study the "critics" of the ancient Western thinkers (e.g. Plato, Augustine) on the epics, especially in the aftermath of the renaissance.

Name: Topics in European Literature
Introduction: This course is a Master ' s postgraduate subject study course aimed at in-depth study of classic writers of European literature. The focus of specific studies depends on the direction of the teaching teacher, and in recent years the main focus has been on Virgil and Dante to help students understand the context of European literature and the blood relationship between English literature and European literature.

Name: Studies in the Contemporary American Novel
Introduction: The course is a research course for senior masters and doctoral students, who have chosen to study American novels in the 20th century or have the corresponding knowledge. The course aims to broaden the selection of thesis by guiding students to read and discuss outstanding works, helping them to learn about the creation of novels in the United States and recent developments in their research, deepening their understanding of American literature.

Name: Twentieth-Century British Women Novelists
Introduction: The course will focus on 20 world English women novelists, through the study of novels, to learn about the creation and cultural and social thinking involved in women ' s 20th century novels in England. The study of novels will be accompanied by the incorporation of feminism into the presentation, which will inform students of the critical and developmental perspectives of feminism and its organic use in the interpretation of women ' s works.

Name: Studies in Gothic Literature
Introduction: The course provided students with an overview of the evolution and evolution of Goth literature from the beginning of the eighteenth century to the centuries of the twentieth century. As an initial popular literature style, the Gothic literature has evolved in many ways over the centuries and has provided us with a rich perspective for its study. In its twisted history of development, Gothic literature has not only experienced cross-nationalism, cross-cultural communication and dissemination, but has also produced a different degree of convergence with literature carriers such as Romans, long novels, romantic poetry, and even magazines, which will be used as an entry point for specific works to study these differences in Goth literature. At the same time, the course will introduce students to the main schools, perspectives and front-line research perspectives of Goth literature research, taking into account specific work. As in the case of Gothic literature, the study of Gothic literature has also gone through a process of development, from early formalism to later historicalism, psychological analysis, etc., and the research perspective of Gothic literature has been in a dynamic process of change, and the course will provide you with an overview of the insights and possible blind spots that these perspectives offer us.

Name: African Cultural Studies
Introduction: From the early nineteenth century to the present, African culture has undergone a dramatic transformation from traditional to modern societies. African cultures have undergone intense renewal and change. An essential link has emerged in the chain of development of African cultures: the transition between tradition and modernity, and the transformation between traditional and modern cultures. In the course of conflict and slow integration between East and West cultures, African countries have introduced Western cultures, transformed traditional cultures, completed the alternation and transformation of old and new cultures and built new systems of discourse. As Western cultures enter African countries, African cultures, although increasingly “Westernized”, continue to explore the broader ways and paths of national cultures in the midst of traditional and modern, Eastern and Western, and national and world conflicts, with the emergence of a group of thinkers with worldwide influence, with a vision of world culture, with a spirit of “willings to transcend”, with a commitment to national spirituality and the pursuit of national aesthetic styles, and with an individuality to break the world pattern of the “European Centre for Literature”. The purpose of the course, which is to provide students with an in-depth understanding of African culture and to contribute to a new era of East-West dialogue, pluralist symbiotic life and universal cultural ties, is to provide an in-depth analysis of the meaning, role and impact of African culture, taking into account specific topics in the field of African culture. Name: High Victorian Britain: Literature and Art in the 1850s
Introduction: Historicists saw the 1950s as the height of Victorian England. During this period, Britain held a Universal Expo, a decade of great strength. This period can be said to have been the most colorful decade of British literature and art, starting with Alfred Dinnison's Memorial, Charles Dickens' David Copefield and Rafael's former Brotherhood, and ending with the amazing design of George Elliott's Adam Bide, Charles Darwin's Origin of Species and William Morris. In fact, all the great Victorian writers during this period were at the peak of their creations, resulting in the emergence of a number of important works, including Dickens ' mega-authors of the 1950s, which criticized Britain ' s arrogance, Browning ' s poems " Men and Women " , Arnold ' s main poems, Tinyson ' s " Mod " and " King ' s Phrase " , Sacre ' s " Newcomons " , Trorop ' s first " Bachest novels " , Newman ' s "The University Concepts " , Muller ' s " Freedom of Expression " and Roskin ' s " The Nature of Gothic Building " . At the same time, this decade is also the most important period of feminist literature. Among the works that emerged during this period were Charlotte Brandt's Villette, Elizabeth Gaskel's Charlotte Brandt's Life, Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Aurora Lee and Christina Rosetti's Monster Fair.

Introduction:
This is a course on Italian language with notions of Italian history and culture taught through communicative methods. There will therefore be a stronger focus on communication, and grammar will mainly be learned through the use of language in class rather than just by learning normative grammar rules.
For this reason, it is very important that students buy an Italian-Chinese (or English-Italian for those confident with English) dictionary and carry it always with them from the very first lesson. Any edition will be fine.

Name: The Bible, Literature and History
Introduction: The course is divided into two main parts. The first part focuses on the main ways in which the Bible was read in the twentieth century, including history tests, literary studies, feminism, post-colonial interpretation, etc. The second part deals with the interpretation and acceptance of the Bible in the history of the West, focusing on its multifaceted effects on Western politics and history at important historical stages. The topic concerned the impact of the Bible in the British civil war, the American abolition campaign and psychological analysis.

Name: African Literature and Culture: Frontier Issues
Introduction: The course offers a project-building (innovation capacity-building) programme for postgraduate courses at Beijing University. The course is designed to explore the intellectual and theoretical resources of the third world and to train students in research methodology and academic writing skills, while introducing them to cutting-edge Asian-African literature critical theories. The first part of the course featured presentations on key research topics related to African literary, cultural and social studies currently in need of construction in the country, exploring the possibility of interaction between China and Asia-Africa Latin America and the African continent in particular at the intellectual and intellectual levels. The course is no longer concerned with the history of literature in Western classic African literature textbooks of the last century and guides students in their theoretical exploration by learning to engage in, understand and criticize the growing diversity of African literature and cultural production and circulation paradigms, such as African literature in the new century, popular culture and youth cultural practices in West, East and Southern Africa. In the latter part of the course, emerging scholars in the fields of Asian-African literature, language and intellectual culture were invited to present the cutting-edge themes and research methods of their participation. Methodological and writing guidelines are being developed for the individual research orientation of students; the ideal goal of the course is to help each graduate student to write a paper of the highest level of publishing.

Language-based quantitative analysis is not only a linguistic research tool but also a mode of thinking. It provides not only an important foundational knowledge and scientific research methodology for students to solve practical problems, but also good training in interdisciplinary thinking. Schoolteachers have systematically studied and studied this field during their studies and have been the first holders of doctoral degrees in this field, writing numerous papers and writing related monographs in this field.

Name: Modern Korean Literary History in Comparative Perspective
Introduction: The main purpose of this course is to develop a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the literary phenomena, representative writers and their representative works in the near modern literary history of Korea, by systematically comparing the history of the near modern Korean (DPRK) literature with the history of the near modern Chinese literature and related works, from a perspective of comparison with the history of the near modern Chinese literature, and by systematically studying the historical processes of the development of the near modern Korean literature history, and to find a comparison of the development context of the near modern Korean literature by comparing it with the development context of the near modern Korean literature; and to develop the basic analytical capacity for literary research by reading and analysing specific works. In addition, the course will organize the current status of research on near-modern literature in the Republic of Korea, as well as research on some of Korea ' s major writers ' works in near-modern literature. This course aims to provide students with a solid foundation for near-modern literary research by systematically comparing the history of near-modern Korean literature with the results of relevant research.

Name: Studies in Burmese Culture
Introduction:
This course provides an overview of the origins of the Myanmar nation, the Indian culture, and the spread and influence of Chinese culture in Myanmar.
Culture, dress culture, eating culture, architecture art, music and dance, traditional competition, ethics, Myanmar
General cultural characteristics, etc. Reference to articles written in Chinese and Chinese, monographs for the development of Myanmar culture
It also has an understanding of the impact on the social, political and economic development of Myanmar.

Name: Studies in Thai History and Present Conditions
Academic Research Methods and Introduction to Oriental Studies Theses
Introduction: The purpose of this course is to improve the academic awareness and research skills of students. The first is the general methodology for the presentation of academic research, including the exploration of academic research methods; the analysis and evaluation of research results from previous generations; the synthesis and innovation of academic perspectives; the discovery, collection, collation and application of research materials; and the norms governing the writing of academic papers. Thematic discussion at the end of the period in conjunction with the study of monographs: Preliminary analysis by students of selected research results (including degree papers) on Oriental studies published in the open academic world. In the classroom, the student sample is evaluated by the acting teacher as a model for different research methods.

Name: Case Studies and Fieldwork in Southeast Asian Culture
Introduction: I. Basic objectives Through a large number of classic cases of socio-cultural research in South-East Asia, knowledge of basic methods and practice models of field surveys, learning of research methods combined with field surveys, and enhancement of academic research capabilities and theoretical perspectives for future South-East Asian cultural studies in field surveys in target countries. II. ELEMENTS OF EDUCATION In the international academic community, socio-cultural research in South-East Asia is important. South-East Asia, as a world-renowned national and religious museum, is a treasure for human cultural diversity, a field park for anthropologists and folklore scientists, a rich ethnic group in South-East Asia (more than 100 nationalities in the Philippines, more than 300 nationalities, tribes in Indonesia, more than 30 nationalities in Thailand, 49 nationalities in Laos, more than 20 nationalities in Cambodia, 54 nationalities in Viet Nam and 135 nations in Myanmar), displays a diverse and endemic culture that attracts the attention of a large number of eminent scholars of Western humanities and social sciences, many of whose findings have become classic research cases, providing vivid research cases for the disciplines of anthropology, history, politics, folklore and religious science in international academia. Thus, reading and understanding of texts in the fields has become an important means of socio-cultural research in South-East Asia through a master-style field survey. The aim of this course is to combine theoretical learning, literature study and field survey practice by using examples of case studies from socio-cultural studies in South-East Asia, through an interactive discussion based on an extensive reading of multidisciplinary case studies, in order to understand case-based socio-cultural research methods, explore the content and outreach of field survey methods, and reflect on the practical ways in which text reading and field surveys work. Future information-gathering missions to target countries could be used to integrate field surveys and empirical research into academic research and writing. The curriculum and content of the course are based on the selected literature, generally reading a book on a one-to-two-week basis, with or without other relevant papers. III. Pedagogical approach Pre-school reading of academic literature, classroom grouping of subject reports and interactive seminars. III. Name: Topics in Southeast Asian Studies: History and Theory
Introduction:
The course focused on the historical, theoretical and methodological aspects of research in South-East Asia in the near 1960s. Bibliography will select monographs and papers from countries in South-East Asia on representation at various stages of development. The materials and perspectives examined were interdisciplinary and balanced with history, theory and methodology.
The form of teaching is combined with the requirement for pre-school reading preparation, submission of book reports and classroom discussions. The aim is to provide international academic developments and training methods for research in Asia, particularly in South-East Asia. Given that the selected material is mainly in English, a better reading base and time guarantee in English is required.

Name: Academic Writing in Southeast Asian Studies
Introduction: This writing course is a mandatory subject for successful graduate students in the South-East Asia Faculty of the Foreign Language Institute and is aimed at training students in basic academic work in research in South-East Asia, with a focus on improving their academic writing skills. The focus of the course is not on the systematic presentation of knowledge points or literature in the relevant fields, but rather on the individual research interests of the selected students, providing them with guidance in the selection of subjects, research design, information search, material organization, writing techniques and publishing strategies. In order to ensure the smooth running of the course, students are required to complete their homework in a timely manner for the review of their teachers and classmates, and to actively participate in the evaluation of other people ' s practices within and outside the classroom. The main aims of the course, which is practice-based, are: 1. To develop awareness of problems and scientific research planning; 2. To identify sources of information relevant to the subject of research; 3. To discuss research methods critically; 4. To learn the organization and use of first-hand and second-hand literature; 5. To become familiar with writing norms and academic ethics; 6. To improve the ability to make written and oral presentations in academic languages.

Name: Studies in Southeast Asian Folk Literature
Introduction: I. Basic objectives South-East Asia is the world-renowned museum of peoples and the treasure of human cultural diversity. For a long time, they have been important subjects of research, anthropologists and field surveys, providing another classic case for research in folklore and folklore worldwide. Folklore and the corresponding folklore culture in South-East Asia, made up of all the countries of the region, the folklore and folklore cultures of all nations, are important components of the culture of the South-East Asian region, are central to the understanding of traditional, popular and multi-ethnic societies in South-East Asia and are a window for the full expression of the diversity and diversity of national cultures in the region. Most of the graduate students targeted by the course have studied the national literature of a South-East Asian country, mastered the language of a South-East Asian country, and learned about the individual folklore in that country. Further learning has helped to broaden the knowledge of the regional culture of South-East Asia, the basic theoretical knowledge of folklore and folklore disciplines and the practical integration of folklore and folklore in South-East Asian countries. II. ELEMENTS OF EDUCATION The teaching content of the curriculum is divided into different topics and the topics set up include three components: The first part is on a country-by-country basis, on a country-by-country basis, on topics such as Viet Nam, Thailand, Myanmar, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, which have established their own specializations. This category of country-specific topics is comprehensive in nature and is designed to provide students with a macro, panorama view of folklore by country in the countries of South-East Asia. The second part is devoted to the cultural phenomena of the representative folklore in the South-East Asian region, which go beyond country-specific constraints and look at these particular cultural phenomena from the perspective of modern folklore. This part, on the one hand, helps to look at the core and representative points of the culture of the South-East Asian region from the perspective of folklore, such as the story of Rome in South-East Asia, the folklore of the southern island peoples, the oral intangible cultural heritage of South-East Asia, the folklore and culture of the indigenous peoples, and, on the other hand, the culture of diversity among the peoples of South-East Asia as a whole, and attempts to explore and study. The third part deals with more theoretical knowledge and academic research topics such as fundamentals and theoretical schools of folklore, anthropological methods and field surveys of folklore research in South-East Asia, which are designed to teach modern folklore theory and to select some of the national and international academic communities - In particular, Western academia, which has more academic results, The classic results and writings of research on folklore and folklore in South-East Asia have placed folklore and folklore in South-East Asia in a broader academic context and on a higher platform of humanities and social sciences, from a simple understanding of some cultural phenomena to a rational analysis and deeper understanding using academic perspectives and disciplines. Introduction: Presentation and presentation of monographs and papers on Myanmar linguistics and literature, knowledge of the current state of research in Myanmar linguistics and Myanmar literature, major genres, debates, and exploration of topics and areas for further research.

Name: General Thai (I)
Introduction: This course is taught mainly in Thai language for zero basic graduate students.

Name: Southeast Asian Cultural Studies
Introduction: The teaching of different cultures in South-East Asia includes topics such as religious culture, etiquette culture, dress culture, eating culture, architecture culture, art ethics and values, as well as the spread and influence of the four cultural circles of China, India, the Arab and the West in the region, giving students an insight into the cultural commonalities of South-East Asia and the special cultural phenomena of the countries of South-East Asia, as well as the history of cultural interaction between countries and other regions. Students are able to read books designated by their teachers and independently accumulate material on certain cultural phenomena, leading to the writing of thought-provoking papers.

Name: Second Language Acquisition
Introduction: The first is centred on second-language learners (teachers), who present three main elements: internal factors of learners, external factors of learners and language of learners. Internal factors include learner ' s linguistic ability, intelligence, starting age, gender, motivation, strategy, style and personality. External factors include social environment, family environment, classroom environment, teaching methods, etc. The language of the learner, i.e. Interlanguage, includes the content, characteristics, development patterns, etc. On the basis of the above, the course continued to introduce second-language learning theory and research methods. The theoretical component consists mainly of congenital, environmental and interactive theories. The methodology section focuses on comparative analysis, bias analysis, language use analysis and speech analysis.

Name: Doctoral Dissertation Seminar
Introduction:
The course helps students form and explore the selection of doctoral thesis and provide support for its advancement and completion. At the beginning of the course, teachers will outline the basic outline and the process of writing degree thesis. Students then report on their selection in turn, discuss their ideas, framework, relevant literature, research methods, etc. in their classes, and gradually adjust, refine or give up their choice.
In addition to providing macro-level guidance and appropriate specific help, regular discussion sessions help students to complete their degree thesis on time in a context of collective support and encouragement.

Name: English Language Teaching Methodology
Introduction: The English Language Teaching Act is one of the core courses of postgraduate studies in the language orientation of English faculties at higher education institutions. The aim is to develop the theoretical basis and practical methods of teaching and studying languages. This course is aimed at the practical aspects of Chinese English language education in the digital age. It helps students to acquire advanced linguistic teaching theory and methodology through both teaching and research practices, and to become familiar with relevant web-based multimedia technologies, and to improve their teaching and scientific skills in English.

Name: Studies in Language and Culture
Introduction: Discussion of classic works and recent results on languages and culture, and introduction of new research issues.

Name: World Englishes
Introduction:
This course introduces theories, models and key concepts in the fields of World Englishes and ELF, investigates the ideological issues associated with the
pluralization of English into Englishes (i.e. from one imperial language into various nativized varieties of English), and examines the development of Chinese Englishes and the implications of WE and ELF research on English education in the Chinese context. By the end of the course, you will be able to explain and critique various WE and ELF theories and models; analyze the ideological issues associated with the spread of English around the world; and conduct original research relevant to WE and ELF research in the Chinese context.

Name: Comparison and Correction of Translations
Introduction:
This course is aimed at building the capacity of graduate students specializing in translation to screen for errors in English translations.
The text of the course focuses on translations in multidisciplinary fields such as philosophy, politics, law, ethics, trade, technology and literature.
This is done by selecting translations of important works (mostly classics) in the above-mentioned fields of study for careful analysis, comparison, identification of their merits, identification of their shortcomings and guidance to students on methods to justify errors in translation.
Owing to the limited time available for the course, the reviews, corrected text materials are mostly selected for classic writings and appear in English and Chinese.
The course is conducted in a combination of lectures. Teachers conduct theoretical analyses and text-based pros and cons, and students should complete the screening and correction of several translation errors within the prescribed time frame. The course requires that, after completing the course, participants be able to acquire basic skills in the theory and techniques of examining and correcting translations.

Name: Literature Search and Thesis Writing
Introduction: The aim of the undergraduate programme is to help students acquire basic knowledge of literature and basic methods of literature search, as well as knowledge and skills in academic writing in practice. The course requires students to experience first-hand the entire process of searching for relevant literature information in the library or on the Internet, while at the same time, under the direction of the teacher, learning to write academic papers in accordance with the general academic norms of the academic community. Students are required to make two oral reports on the literature search in the course of a semester and to complete a term paper.

Name: Comprehensive Practicum
Introduction: This course is a comprehensive practical course for postgraduate students with master ' s degree in translation. It is designed to provide students with a platform for direct participation in translation practice and, under the guidance of the teacher, to understand and grasp the nature of the work of professional translators, their professional norms and the required professional qualities and professional conduct of professional translators through specific translation projects. The course will be based on Chinese-language writings in humanities and social sciences, or other texts related to practical projects, designated by the mentor, who will provide real-time guidance and grade them in stages, depending on the student ' s quantitative translation. The overall rating is ultimately given by the mentor. In order to enhance the training of graduate students in master ' s degree in translation and professional skills, they are required to complete the reading and examination of the standard book of general education prior to graduation (generally in the first academic year).

Name: Translation Practice I: English-Chinese Translation
Introduction: The course is intended for Masters of Translation students, who are required to have a strong basic English language skills, to reach out to different styles of translation practice and to acquire higher professional translation skills through a one-term course.

Name: Translation Practice IV
Introduction: The course requires students to perform their own translation (in Chinese) of 4,000 words per month (excluding vacation months) in the first school year; translation is done by a graduate student. Post-graduate students should select the humanities content; the selected source text should have no published translations (including those posted online); the source text should be appropriate for published English books.

Name: Translation Practice I: Advanced English-Chinese Translation
Introduction: The course is a follow-up course to the theoretical study of translation. It is intended to enable students to conduct practical and research studies of English and Chinese translations based on a combination of “translation theory” knowledge, to develop advanced English and Chinese translation skills, mainly for literary translation, and to study the appreciation and comparison of English and Chinese languages and cultures. The course is based on the practice of text translation and is guided by the basic theory of contemporary English language and linguistics and translation, as well as by the academic background of the basic knowledge and basic research skills of the students attending the English specialty undergraduate linguistics and literature courses. Teaching is dominated by theoretical teaching, interpretation demonstrations and classroom discussions. Due to the high level of practicality of the course, students are required to teach 5-6 English translations during the school year (the subject is assigned by the teacher) as the basis for evaluating the results of the course, which is 40 per cent of the course ' s achievement; the final examination is divided into two parts: 1) English/Han translation, which is guided by the theory of translation and evaluates the merits of a given translation; and 2) English/Han translation, which is about 300 words.

Name: Human Resource Management
Introduction: Topics: The Human Resources Management course is the science of theory, principles and methods for developing human resources, improving their quality and rationalizing their use. It is a basic professional course designed to develop the basic theory, knowledge and competence of students in human resources management. The objectives of the course are: to make students aware of the role of human resources in economic and social development; to acquire the basic theory, basic knowledge and basic methods of human resources management; to develop the capacity to engage in human resources management; and to lay the foundation for learning and future work in other professional subjects.

Name: Primate Behavior, Society and Evolution
Introduction: Why has humankind evolved so successfully? Perhaps we can get some clues from our human cousins, the inhuman primates. The primates, the size of all things, are the more special category of mammals, and now number as many as 500. The behaviour of primates is diverse and highly socialized and is inextricably linked to human beings. Research into primate behaviour and society helps us to understand animal and human behaviour, its origins and evolution. The curriculum is based on the fifth edition of the book Primate Behavior Ecology, by the world ' s renowned primateist Karen B. Strier, and students can learn not only about basic primate behaviour, social structure and its evolutionary history, but also about the latest scientific findings and develop interest in research in primate behavioral ecology. Through this course, students are required to reflect on the evolution of the social and behavioural development of animals and humans and to explore the origins of human nature, based on the knowledge of the evolutionary history and diversity of primates, their social structure and behaviour characteristics and their strategies, functions and diversity.

Name: English-Chinese Text Compilation
Introduction:
The purpose of the course is to train students in the political aspects of current affairs, to conduct anatomy, analysis and generalization of each course on a case-by-case basis, to organize classroom discussions among students, to enable them to learn about the English-Handian translation progressively through case studies and to improve the actual translation capacity by completing a certain number of translations.
The course requires students to read a certain number of cases and other materials before each session and to answer and discuss relevant questions in the classroom. Students are also required to submit, within the prescribed time frame, five compilations, three for English and two for Han, on subjects prescribed by the teacher or chosen by the student.

Name: Modern History of Translation and Translation Theory
Introduction:
The course consists of both translation history and translation theory. In terms of translation theory, in addition to presenting important theories at home and abroad, the lecturers, in accordance with the special circumstances of Chinese students, have focused more on practical translation theory, such as the nature of translation, translation principles, translation standards, translation processes, types of translation techniques, etc., with a view to explaining the phenomena of translation of various types and guiding specific translation practices. The course emphasizes the translation practice of the Service to underpin translation theory and, as a result, there is a great deal of translation practice within the course, guided by translation principles, translation standard theory, which brings theory into line with skills training.
The course is equipped with a rich body of practice topics containing examples of translations of classic literature in humanities and social sciences for use by learners. The course is given more time for translation skills training. Theoretically, as far as possible, it takes place in a combination of positive presentations and classroom discussions.

Name: Fundamentals of English Interpretation
Introduction:
This course is a limited selection course for postgraduate students with master ' s degrees in translation.
As the teaching content focuses mainly on the development of practical skills for conference interpretation, better English-han bilingual hearing and expression skills and relatively stable psychological qualities form the basis for successful learning.
The course will begin with a presentation on the development history of interpretation at meetings, basic concepts, working modalities and quality evaluation criteria. At the same time, clarification is given of the cognitive and psychological processes of conference interpretation (including alternation and simultaneous interpretation) and of the multi-tasking model of interpretation practice, such as hearing understanding in alternate interpretation, interaction between memory and notes, reorganization of translation information and expression, long-, short-term memory mechanisms in simultaneous interpretation, power allocation, etc.
On this basis, the course will present the key elements and methods of training in conference interpretation skills, including the hearing and memory of alternate interpretation, subject matter analysis, notes, shadow exercises for simultaneous interpretation, visualization, generalization and abbreviation techniques, and will be complemented by appropriate and tailored hands-on training.
The purpose of this course is to lay the foundations for a good thinking and training methodology for the future transition of students to higher-level professional interpretation training.

Name: Fundamentals of Translation Technology Practice
Introduction: An introductory course on translation techniques for master ' s degree in translation, with emphasis on practical and applied skills, requires students to acquire effective ways and tools to access professional information in the information age, mastery of mainstream search engines and computer-assisted translation tools or systems, flexibility in the application of a wide range of information technology and professional translation skills, and efficient solutions to common problems encountered in translation practice and translation. Students taking this course are required to have the basics of computer operations and web applications.

Name: China's Relations with Neighboring Regions
Introduction: China's Relations with Periphery is one of the core courses of the Foreign Language Institute of Beijing University in the field of “Country and Regional Studies” and is designated as a compulsory master's and doctoral degree course in the direction of national and regional studies, open to other undergraduate and graduate students throughout the school. This course complements that of Regional and Country Studies: Theory and Methodology, and is designed to present specific historical and current issues in the target region to Ph.D. students specializing in “Country and Regional Studies”. Based on the composition of the teaching team, the two modules of the course will include a presentation on the history and status of North-East Asia, South-East Asia, South Asia, West Asia, Central Asia and North Asia. On the basis of the history and current situation of the target region, the course also emphasizes the historical interaction and current diplomatic relations between China and those regions, with the aim of preparing students to understand the affairs of the target region from the perspective of the country ' s position and diplomatic relations. The course will be divided into two main modules according to the duration of the semester. The first module focuses on history and describes the historical exchanges and interactions between China and the surrounding region, and it is planned that each of the course teachers will teach the historical links between the respective subject area and China. The module will provide a platform for doctoral students to study and study the historical background of specific issues in the target region. Important country and regional issues at the moment often involve complex historical contexts. While learning about historical research methods, the module will provide graduate students with an opportunity to deepen the historical background of research topics and provide a more solid basis for future writing of doctoral thesis. The second module is formally similar to the first, but focuses on contemporary diplomatic relations between China and the surrounding region. Each classroom teacher may introduce one or more aspects of political, economic or human exchange, or select an important diplomatic event as a case study, examine problems in China ' s dealings with the region and explore future trends. Module III designs reports and discussions for student course papers. Postgraduate students studying this course need to reflect on and select specific topics related to the subject of the course in the course, to design an outline of the paper and research methodology, to prepare a bibliography on it and to present its research design in the module, to discuss with teachers and classmates, and to finalize the course papers on time.

Name: Comparative Rhetoric and Translation Practice
Introduction: This course provides a basis for students to learn more about the important effects of Western rhetorical traditions in translating such intercultural communication by studying the foundational writings of the Chinese-Western rhetorical tradition and important academic articles, by understanding and mastering the basic concepts of Chinese-Western rhetoric and writing tradition, and by analysing and comparing differences and differences from a comparative rhetorical point of view. Having become familiar with the important concepts of the Chinese-Western rhetoric and writing tradition, teachers have led students to further examine the impact of language characteristics, traditional ways of thinking, aesthetic concepts and the order in which information is expressed on translation practice from a comparative perspective, and to understand from a practical point of view the relevance of research on comparative rhetoric and cultural differences to translation practice.

Name: Language Service Project Management
Introduction:
The course is intended to provide participants with an in-depth knowledge and understanding of the current situation and trends in the translation market and the project management process and knowledge architecture for translation. Trainees are trained in the effective use of translation project management software, combined with project management practices, while having a bilingual understanding and expression capability and a multidisciplinary professional background.
The trainees should have a basic course of translation and basic computer skills.

Name: The United Nations and International Organizations
Introduction: 1. Development history of States and international organizations; 2 Theory of international organizations in Western international relations; 3 The relationship between international organizations and the international order; 4 The status and role of the United Nations in international politics; 5 The impact of the three major economic organizations on world economic development; 5 Regionalization and regional organizations; 6 China and international organizations

Name: Comparison of Chinese and Western Cultures
Introduction: Opening of the course: The purpose of this course, which is intended primarily for graduate students of the Institute of World Literature, is to enable them to have a broader cultural perspective, especially in comparison with Western and Central cultures, while pursuing world literary studies. The course is designed to guide graduate students in the direction of their research activities as far as possible. Basis of the course: The course has been offered for 14 consecutive years as an elective and general course for students at the North University undergraduate level. The lecturers have accumulated many useful experiences and a large number of systematic courses in the course of their long courses. Since the beginning of the course, the course has been popular and has been accredited as an excellent general selection at Beijing University. In addition, the lecturer served as moderator of the project entitled " Comparative study of Western and Central culture " , a research project set up at the Northern Grand Outer House. The result of the project, Comparative Introduction to Central West Culture, has been published by Beijing University Press (2007). The course has also been taught by lecturers at 100 forums on central television and at the Department of Logistics of the State Department. Based on a number of the above-mentioned conditions, the actual content of the course has been carefully refined and deepened and formally applied for postgraduate studies. Course introduction: This course is mainly a theoretical comparison of several important aspects of Western and Central culture. First of all, the difference and comparison between the Chinese and Western languages (Chinese and Indo-European languages, especially English) are taken into account, leading to a macro-comparison of the theoretical differences in the focus between more than a dozen disciplines, such as Central and Western geography, philosophy, aesthetics, law, ethics, literature, economics, science and technology, medicine, religion and education, from which the regularities are identified, enabling the participants to grasp the essence of Western and Central culture from the macro as a whole and provide them with a number of guiding macro-background knowledge for their future micro-studies in a particular field. In our country, comparative cultural science is an emerging subject, which is particularly relevant and necessary for current graduate students, who have the advantage of foreign languages and have the ability to read the relevant literature in Western languages to varying degrees directly, which provides the most favourable conditions for the smooth running of the course; on the other hand, since in recent decades all our universities have paid little attention to the general macro-knowledge transfer of Western and Central culture in their curricula, so that some of their students are trained as mere resource persons, and have a relative lack of basic macro-level cultural knowledge and theoretical literacy, which, despite many of them, is less general. So the course is very relevant as an attempt to provide some kind of brick-throwing for the future of my school.

Name: Modernization Theory and China's Modernization
Introduction: The course will explore the process and main elements of the theory of modernization in the world and will use the theory of modernization as the analytical framework, analyse the historical process of modernization in China, streamline China ' s modernization thinking, take stock of the lessons learned from China ' s modernization and explore the path and patterns of modern development in China. The main teaching elements of the course include: the content of the concept of modern theory; the genres and views of classical modern theory; dependence, the theory of the world system, the theory of post-modernism; the latest developments in modern theory; why China has not been the first to change modernity; the historical process of modernization in China; the modern thinking of China; farmers ' issues and China ' s modernization process; traditional culture and China ' s modernization; and the status and problems of China ' s modernization. The course, which is primarily taught, is complemented by classroom discussions and seeks to provide students with a basic understanding of modern theory and the history and reality of modern China.

Name: Contemporary Interpretations of Classic Marxist Concepts
Introduction: Marxism is a theoretical system of many concepts, which cannot be fully equated in the context of classical writers and in the context of contemporary Chinese realities, and which need to be restructured and enriched as necessary. The course is intended to be a topical one, with an age- and Chinese-oriented elaboration of important concepts and areas. It involves: class, proletariat, bourgeois, middle class, people, masses, citizens, freedoms, democracy, justice, socialism, communism, revolution, capital, worship.

Name: The Eastward Spread of Western Learning and China's Modernization
Introduction: This course deals with the impact of Western culture on China ' s modernization in the face of Master ' s degree studies in Marxist Chinese Studies, with the process of East China ' s studies and the history of China ' s modernization as major leads. A more in-depth presentation will be made of the historical stage of the West School Graduation, the historical trajectory of China ' s modernization and the important role of West School Graduation in China ' s modernization. The course will inspire students to review the interaction between Western and traditional Chinese cultures, the relevance of culture to social, economic and national development, reflect on the history and reality of China ' s modernization and look forward to the way forward in China ' s modernization path.

Name: Topics in Comparative Values Education
Introduction: The curriculum will focus primarily on education on political ideology, cultural identity and cultural understanding, and moral education, as included in values education, and will examine the nature, characteristics, content, systems and methods of education on values in the world ' s major countries and cultural groups.

Name: Nietzsche's Philosophy

Name: Selected Readings in Frontier Works on the Cultural Industries
Introduction: Culture is a central expression of the human way of life and a symbol of the collective values and aesthetic thinking of the members of society, using patterns of painting, music, sculpture, film, television, cultural heritage to reflect the spiritual, spiritual, ceremonial, legal, etc. of a people or region. Culture, creativity and industry began a historic union, driven by modern market economies and high-tech technologies. Whether it is Western tradition or Chinese history, “culture”, “creativeness” and “industry” fall into different tributaries in a long history. In the cultural and economic era of the post-industrial society, the tributaries of “Cultural Water”, “Creative Water”, and “Industry Water” are collating rivers of “Creative Creative Industries”. The cultural industry, as an emerging industry chosen by countries and regions that are highly developed in post-industrial societies, modern services, is an industrial upgrading of the modern society towards a post-modern society. It is well known that modernization pursues modern societies, that is, industrial societies, whose main mode of growth is the material growth of industrialism; post-modern societies, that is, post-industrial societies, whose growth patterns have shifted towards culturalism, and production goals have shifted from the unrestricted exploitation of natural resources by industrial societies to the use of cultural resources by post-industrial societies. As human society enters the age of cultural economy, including China, the cultural industry has become the largest in the new century in developed and emerging countries. Large industry imaginations and capital wonders, culture seems to be entering the harmony between the traditional notion of “culture as a platform, economic singing” and the harmony between “culture” and “economic” cosmopolitan music, and cultural industries have become the main means of boosting economic confidence, transforming economic growth patterns and promoting industrial development. Culture emphasizes history, creativity emphasizes real innovation, industry emphasizes the size of the economy and the application of technology, and “culture”, “creative” and “industry” are contradictory concepts and contain opposing factors: Cultural heritage can be a barrier to innovation, and standardized industrial approaches can undermine cultural creativity. When they're moving, “culture” conveys “the thickness of what they want”, “creative” emphasizes “the depth of what they want” and “industry” highlights “the breadth of what they seek to accept”. “Creative” makes “culture” an “industry”. In the history of the development of the cultural industry for more than 100 years, how has culture been able to disintegrate the elitist veil and enter the popular experience of entertainment? How can the cultural industry experience a heavy fire and enter the highest levels of decision-making by Governments? In this history and reality, the course looks at the fundamental logic and theoretical controversy of the cultural industry by retrogressing the classics of modern humanist art thinking, cultural sociology, cultural economics and art management. The curriculum is divided into four parts: (a) First, to clarify the concepts and content of mechanical reproduction of terms such as art, cultural industry, cultural industry, creative industry, etc., in different time contexts and social settings; (b) Second, reflect on the linkages and contradictions between cultural and commercial economics in the development of cultural industries; (c) Thirdly, to discuss social practices related to cultural industries and cultural convergence, creative parks and cities; Fourth, we look at the social implications and economic benefits of developing cultural industries in Asia (South Korea, Japan), the Americas (United States), Europe (United Kingdom, France, Germany) and mainland China and Taiwan.

Name: Advertising Criticism
Introduction: Advertising criticism is a theoretical course closely linked to practice. It trains students in the combined interpretation, analysis and criticalisation of the current advertising industry, advertising works and advertising phenomena. Advertising history, advertising principles and advertising criticism are important components of the modern advertising research system. Among them, advertising is critical of subjects different from the history of advertising, namely advertising works, advertising phenomena, advertising practices, advertisers, etc. If advertising history research is a reflection and a reflection, advertising criticism is a visualization and interpretation of what is happening now. The subject of advertising criticism is critics with a certain level of advertising. While everyone can understand advertising, not everyone can engage in advertising criticism. Advertising critics must have a higher degree of judgement and standards than the public at large or even the general advertising profession, so that they can make an accurate judgement and guide the development of the advertising industry. In terms of knowledge structure, it requires researchers to be both deep and distant, i.e., deeply involved, understood and determined in the industry, while at the same time maintaining a sober mind and an independent spirit, so that they can emerge from the industry for theoretical criticism. The theory of advertising criticism draws on other disciplines, both in terms of the commonality of social phenomena in general and in terms of the advertising profession. Students can therefore learn to be critical in advertising, and in turn use this way of thinking and research across and across other communication phenomena such as visual, artistic, cultural and social. On the other hand, the characteristics of the advertising profession can, in turn, complement the macro-social effects of general literature and art criticism. The course will be conducted in two modules, theoretical and practical. In the theoretical part, the various theories of criticism since the Frankfurt school, such as symbolic criticism, interpretation and acceptance of aesthetic criticism, social criticism, feminism criticism, cultural research criticism, neurology criticism, etc., will be systematically explained. In the practice area, there will be critical case studies on the advertising industry, advertising and creative work, advertising effects, advertising culture, advertising education, etc., taking into account the practical experience of individual teachers in critical work. The arrangements are as follows (tentative): First, the object of the advertisement, the criteria and the problem. Second, the advertising body is critical: symbolism, new criticism. Three: Advertising aesthetic criticism: form tower psychology. Fourth, interpretation and acceptance of aesthetic criticism. Fifth, external criticism of advertising: Frankfurt school and social criticism. Sixth, neurology criticism. Seven: Feminism criticism. Eighth, cultural research criticism. Number nine: Advertisement and ethics. The 10th. The ad aesthetic and creative criticism. Advertising industry and advertising effects criticism The ads are critical. The advertising industry is critical. 15: Advertising education criticism Advertising criticism and contemporary advertising history The course is conducted in the form of a combination of teacher lectures and student discussions. Name: Studies in Cultural Economics and Creative Management
Introduction: The shift from culture to industry is bound to lead to a shift from political to cultural economics, and the intersection between economics and cultural research is the result of cultural industry practices. The cultural factor is a factor of economic growth, and the cultural economy is concerned with the form, characteristics and socio-cultural needs of the use of economic patterns in the cultural sphere. Cultural resources can add value to cultural industries by using high-tech technologies, by targeting modern markets and by transforming cultural creativity into cultural products of commodity value. Diversion of resources is a combination of cultural expressions. Cultural resources generated by the transmission of innovation include all historical and cultural resources, including knowledge, beliefs, art, ethics, law, custom and real cultural resources, both material and intangible. The innovation of cultural creative industries is a fundamental feature of the artistic nature of cultural products: creative, quantitative reproduction of original cultural symbols, and the main social function of marketing activities is cultural diffusion. In this way, the cultural creative industry has become an important form of contemporary transformation of human history and culture. Creative ideas include the desire to inspire creativity itself and how to find ways to shape it when it is inspired. In the traditional sense, creativity belongs exclusively to artists. Today ' s society has entered an era of consumption, a business era focused on cultural entertainment, where business and media entertainment seem to have a deeper influence on one ' s consumer perception and cultural behaviour than political and religious power. In this context, creativity is no longer the gift of the individual, but the consensus of the group; creativity is no longer about innovation and innovation, but about “purposeful application” and values; creativity is no longer the result of a sense of thought, but rather the process of multi-think interaction; creativity is no longer the battle of the individual, but the synergy of groups and organizations. Here, creative behaviour plays an equal role with non-conceptive behaviour that leads to creative agreement. Here, the process of consumer behaviour is transformed into an innovative consumption because of the symbolic character of cultural products. Creativeness is shaping a new image of national and regional industries, and the creative power of a people has taken a prominent place among the driving forces of the national economy. Creative management takes into account not only the commercial value of cultural products but also the artistic value of cultural products, which are fundamental to cultural products. The purpose of creative management is to bring cultural products into line with the symbols of the general public, which have meaning and value, feelings and experiences, responsibility and mission. That is the classic of transcending time and becoming history, and that is the myth of transcending space and becoming the world. Creative management is a balancing technique that, in the age of the commodity economy, adheres to the meaning of culture and the value of the market, which is a contradiction of the heritage of human culture, but is the true destiny of its attack. In the context of cultural economy and creative management, the course explores the basic topics of cultural industry operations, such as cultural values, cultural consumption, cultural and artistic cost disorders, soft innovation in cultural industries, creativity and management, creative strategies, creative leadership. The content of the course is divided into the following sections: First, cultural heritage, reproduction flows and value addition; Second, the socio-economic cultural paradigm and the theory of the value of cultural economics; Third, the operation of the cultural industry — sensory artistic creation and rational economic management; Fourth, the operation of cultural industries — symbolic value and experience construction; Fifth, the operation of cultural industries — creative production and organizational management; Sixth, social reflection in cultural industries — symbolic consumption and cultural wonders; Seventh, social reflection of cultural industries: the dialectic of cultural creation and economic innovation; Eighth, cultural economy and urban space; Ninth, cultural space and industry clusters; Tenth, Tourism consumption and regional economies; 11, Creative Manager and Creative Management; Twelfth to fifteenth, comprehensive discussion and typical case analysis

Language assessment and testing is a very practical exercise, and the theory and methodology must be developed through systematic learning and operational exercises.
The objective of the course is to equip graduate students with the basic concepts, basic theories and basic methods of second-language assessment and testing through systematic learning and the operationalization of related tasks.

Name: Psychology of Foreign Language Education
College: School of Chinese as a Second Language
Introduction: Psychiatry in foreign language education is a study of the basic psychological patterns of study and teaching of foreign languages in the school context. It is a branch of teaching psychology in foreign language learning and teaching theory and practice. Its basic research component consists of the psychological aspects of foreign language learning and teaching. Through the study of psychological aspects of learning in foreign languages, students are able to learn about psychological, cognitive and linguistic development patterns, psychological patterns of learning in foreign languages and learning conditions (such as the important role of the individual factor of learning in foreign languages) and the important role of studying the psychological process of learning in foreign languages. This enables students to learn “what to teach” and “how to teach” and to know “why to teach” and “when to teach” and to recognize that they need to focus not only on external teaching factors, such as foreign language teaching methods, but also on the exploration of the learning process, thereby enhancing their scientific and consciousness in teaching foreign language subjects, so that teaching can be consciously based on the theory of learning and the psychological characteristics of foreign language learners in future foreign language teaching. On the other hand, by learning about the psychological content of teaching, pupils are taught about the psychology of teaching, teaching design and classroom management, and students are made aware of the importance of using learning theory in the design of teaching in foreign languages to improve teaching design and classroom management practices and to improve the efficiency and results of teaching. Name: Inhibitory Processes in Attention, Memory and Language
College: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
Introduction:
Depressive control plays a central role in the computational theory of human processing, which can serve both visual or hearing selectivity and human memory and linguistic recognition. Taking into account the latest results of current international cognitive neuroscience studies on inhibition processes, the course provides a systematic introduction to the cognitive and neurological mechanisms of human attention, memory and speech inhibition processes.  
Through this course, students can learn not only about inhibition mechanisms in human cognitive processes, but also further develop the theoretical and methodological literacy of cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience, and provide a good theoretical and methodological basis for future practical work in cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience, or psychological counselling and treatment.
In order to better learn and understand the content of the curriculum, students need to systematically study the basic subjects of experimental psychology (especially experimental design), psychostatistics and cognitive psychology. In addition, students need to be actively involved in classroom discussions, carefully read the documents they have set up and make high-level comments on them.

The cognitive neuroscientific primarily studies the neurological basis of cognitive functions such as perception, attention, memory, language, motor control and consciousness. It is a cross-cutting discipline developed on the basis of a variety of disciplines, including cognitive psychology, neuroscience, computer science and linguistics. The various brain imaging techniques developed in recent years (e.g., high-density event-related electrons, magnetic maps of the brain, positive electron fault scans, functional magnetic resonance and cranial magnetic stimulation) have been combined with traditional psychological studies and have become the main research tools in cognitive neuroscience. The course will combine the scientific work carried out by the teaching teachers to teach up-to-date cognitive neuroscientific research in the fields of consciousness, attention, memory, language, awareness and social awareness, to present the latest research results and the latest research tools and methods, and to inform students about the unique research thinking and methods in this new field.

Through this course, students will have a comprehensive understanding of the concepts and thinking behind the design of digital communication systems when faced with genuine belief, as well as the overall design architecture and programmes.

Introduction: The course will address the basic knowledge of digital communication systems and this concept, including, inter alia, the following. 1) A review of the fundamentals of probabilistic theory and random processes and a study of the expression and application of the relevant theorems in digital communication systems, such as the maximum-comparison problem, the big-digit theorems and the very restrictive of the centre, independence and related definitions, self-relevant functions, the search for interrelate functions, the relationship between self-relative functions and power spectral density, etc. 2) The rationale of the transmitter: its content includes principles for the design of the launch signal wave, as well as limitations; the Naquester guidelines and matching filters; the principles of the base belt digital transfer; and the modem/decomposition. 3) Amnesia-free and memory-based modems: give several forms of memoryless modems, such as PAM, PSK, QAM, OQPSK, and their expressions; the role of time-space protection spacing and design requirements; and several key technologies of the OFDM system. 6) Transport frequency deviations of communication systems: the cause of the carrier frequency deviations and their mathematical description; the impact of the carrier frequency deviations on the single wave system and options for overcoming their effects; the impact of the carrier frequency deviations on the multi-wave system and their solutions; and solutions to reduce the sub-load interference (ICI) of the OFDM system. 7) Sampling clock deviations in the communications system: the cause of sampling clock deviations and their mathematical description; When the laser is broken, we're going to do holograms, in which case we can replace the laser with computers. We will find that the digital hologram has many advantages over the laser hologram, but also some disadvantages, depending on the purpose of the hologram application. The course will begin with a presentation of optical holographic theory and production methods, followed by a presentation of the basic theory of digital holographic technology from the point of view of the telecommunication engineering theory, a re-presentation of methods and types of digital holographic technology, with a focus on the principles and methods of production of the Lohmann type and the interferometric type of digital holographic technology, and finally, an introduction of the application of digital holographic technology in optical information processing, interferometry and the production of digital holographic components.

Name: Fundamentals of Optoelectronics

Introduction: Optoelectronics will undoubtedly play a very important role in the field of applied science in the twenty-first century, as optical electronics are key to high-speed communications. The low-depletion transfer window of the monolithic fibre-optic quartz is as high as 50 THz, a huge bandwidth resource. The current fibre-optic transport capacity is 10.6 Tbit/s. This achievement cannot be separated from advances in optical and electronic technology. In the past few years, remarkable progress has been made in light electronics, including various semiconductor lasers (e.g. quantum quail, quantum line, quantum point lasers), electro-absorption modems, high-speed light detectors, blended fibre-optic amplifiers, fibre-optic rasters, etc., which have high application value in light generation, regulation, transmission, detection and processing. The purpose of this course is to describe the latest optical electronic devices produced by technological advances in recent years and to highlight the physical models, experimental validation, applications and limitations of these electrons.
