Introduction:
Microwave photology is the scientific field of microwave technology and phototechnologies that intersect, studying the principles and applications of interaction between microwave signals and light signals, including the generation, transmission, control and processing of microwave signals.
This course is aimed at graduate and senior undergraduate students in communications and information systems, particularly in the field of fibre-optic communication. Learning about the noise mechanisms of optical electronics in optical communication systems, including lasers, modems, optical amplifiers, optical detectors and noise evolution in fibre-optic links; learning about the generation and measurement of ultra-low noise telecommunication; learning about the microwave photosystem architecture and its application in communication systems. Know the latest forward movement in microwave photology, such as chip photo-frequency combs, chip microwave photosystems, Teherz communications, etc.
Learning through this course requires mastery of the basic idea of microwave optics, i.e., how optical advantages can be exercised and applied in the microwave field; requires mastery of the noise machines of commonly used optical electronics and corresponding mathematical modelling; and understanding of the latest developments in optical optics in microwave optic systems, where one or two experimental programmes embodying optical advantages can be proposed.

Name: Multicore Storage System Architecture
College: School of Electronics Engineering and Computer Science
Introduction: The increasing speed gap between processors and repositories makes the organization, structure and design of storage subsystems an important component of the design of computer systems. Storage-level structures that include both film-based caches and film-based primary and outer deposits are already a key determinant of the overall systematic energy and power consumption of computers. The current multi-nuclear processor will impose higher bandwidth requirements on the storage system, making it important to avoid a piece of off-site storage by increasing the impact of tape caches. The future polynuclear processors will contain a number of large caches that are connected via a piece of network and shared over multiple cores. The course will discuss the knowledge of software and hardware and the latest research results on the organization and management of multi-nuclear caches. In addition, in the current age of big data, cloud computing, machine learning and artificial intelligence, the isomer multinuclear processor has unprecedented access characteristics and huge bandwidth demands, making shared primary and external storage systems one of the hotspot technologies, which mainly cover transmission levels, such as access routes, protocols and request scheduling. Finally, the course will introduce storage techniques associated with emerging storage processes such as non-removable storage. The course focuses on system-level design, logical design and performance indicators for storage systems and will initially address energy costs and security at modern storage levels.

Name: Theory and Systems of Distributed Machine Learning
College: School of Electronics Engineering and Computer Science
Introduction:
The rapid development of artificial intelligence in recent years has benefited from machine learning. In the age of artificial intelligence, the effective use of “big data” and the effective training of “big models” in the face of large machine-learning missions have become important research directions for academia and industry. In the Internet environment, however, assumptions such as the static distribution of data in traditional machine learning, the simpleness of data objects and the complete accuracy of data labelling are no longer valid. In particular, the issue of data privacy has become more prominent in recent years, and the processing of private sensitive data in a more secure, rational and legitimate manner has also posed enormous challenges for machine learning. Distributive machine learning is considered an effective technological tool.
Distributive machine learning is not a simple combination of distributive processing techniques and machine learning. It involves many aspects, including new machine learning models and algorithm design, multi-learning model assembly, data parallel models, cross-over communications, data privacy protection, performance and security. The course will provide an overview of the current state of distributed machine learning to graduate students in the relevant directions from two perspectives of basic theory and system-building, combining the latest academic findings of emerging in-depth studies, migration studies and federal studies, and curriculum project design with actual data and projects at the industrial level.

Name: 3D Reconstruction from Images and Video
College: School of Electronics Engineering and Computer Science
Introduction:
Three-dimensional image/video-based reconstruction is one of the key areas of research in computer science, which is highly practical and applied, and has in recent years given rise to strong life in multidisciplinary application practices through a combination of artificial intelligence, machine learning and virtual reality. The course focuses on the application background, key content, cutting-edge results and developments for the reconstruction of three-dimensional scenes based on images and videos, providing students with basic theoretical knowledge and research thinking in relevant fields. At the same time, it combines theoretical discourse and research dynamics, providing relevant research leads, completing a number of practical topics in the form of thematic discussions and course exercises, encouraging students to solve problems through innovative thinking and practice, and building the capacity of students to be innovative in practice.
Through this course, students are given a degree of depth and breadth in their basic theoretical knowledge and hands-on skills in the field of image- and video-based understanding and analysis, thus enabling them to further study, research and hands-on practice in relevant areas. It also fosters sophisticated and innovative thinking with the capacity to respond to interdisciplinary, cross-sectoral technological challenges and address critical issues at the forefront of industry development.

Name: Video Coding and Understanding
College: School of Electronics Engineering and Computer Science
Introduction: Digital media technology (or multimedia technology) is a cross-cutting subject in computer software and hardware and applications, electronics, communications and broadcasting, and the computer departments of well-known universities in the country and abroad have developed a rich variety of multi-media technology courses covering multimedia content coding, representation, transmission and multimedia equipment and systems, as well as cross-curricular courses in design, art and arts (e.g. the MIT "Media Arts and Science" series). The richness and diversity of the courses played an important role in the development of the digital media discipline, but to some extent masked the underlying technical and theoretical issues. Video is one of the most important forms of media in digital media, and as applications such as digital television, video video, video surveillance and videoconferencing develop, we are ushering in an era of video everywhere. The efficiency of video coding is an important indicator of the development of digital media technology, and automatic video understanding is key to the widespread and in-depth application of big video resources. Currently, the two previously separate fields of research, video encoding and video understanding, are being combined, visual properties and visual understanding are becoming important research directions for increasing the efficiency of video coding, and direct analysis and understanding of post-condensed video is becoming the main means of processing and using big video. The curriculum will be taught from a cross-cutting perspective, and students will benefit from it, regardless of whether their specific research direction is video code or video understanding. This course is a continuation of the undergraduate course entitled " Foundations of Digital Media Technology " , which assumes that students already have visual knowledge of multimedia technologies and systems, mastery of the underlying concepts, learning about video coding and understanding, and learning about the main principles and methods of video coding and understanding, as well as hands-on work to improve the performance of video coding software and participation in international competitions on video retrieval, developing good scientific practices and laying a good foundation for subsequent research.

Name: Economics Thesis Writing
Introduction: Improvement of the level of post-graduate dissertation. Basis of the course: Teachers themselves have written academic papers and books. Students are required to write a shorter, discipline-compliant paper on economics by learning about the relevant norms of writing and by practice and discussion.

Name: Topics in the Chinese Economy
Introduction: Focusing on China's economy. The analysis focused on China ' s land system, land reform in mainland China and Taiwan, the People ' s Commune Movement, economic institutional reform, financial reform and reform of State-owned enterprises.

Name: Frontiers and Research Methods in Economics
Introduction:
The National Institute of Development is committed to promoting comprehensive research in Chinese social sciences, trying to organize interdisciplinary research, cultivating comprehensive senior talents for national development, serving my country's reform and development and the construction of a new global order with comprehensive knowledge collection, and serving the discovery and exploration of social sciences. _x000D_
This course aims to improve students' academic literacy and cultivate students' subject literacy and scientific spirit. It relies on the college's strong professors represented by Lin Yifu, Zhou Qiren, Zhang Weiying, Song Guoqing and other famous teachers, and combines their research fields and research experiences to teach cutting-edge economics theories and research methods. _x000D_

Name: Topics in Economic Research I
Introduction:
From payment services (mobile payments, third-party payments) to network finance (group financing, P2P or electricity provider micro-credit), from channel services (selling of investment goods) to network banking, Internet finance has profoundly affected the economic activities of many Chinese enterprises and individuals.

Is Internet finance only a bubble in the financial reform process, or is it an important force that could transform the traditional financial system?

The purpose of this lecture is to help students understand the reasons for the rise of Internet finance, the resulting benefits and the risks that may arise by exploring important theoretical and practical issues, particularly by distilling cases from some industries, particularly Internet finance enterprises.

Several of the teachers who conducted the course were researchers at the newly established Beijing University Internet Finance Research Centre and were professors at the National Institute for Development Studies.

Name: Methods of Causal Identification in Economic Development
Introduction: Cause-and-effect inference is one of the central methods of empirical economics. This course has two main objectives. The first objective is to become familiar with the basic methods of mastering causal extrapolations, including the double differential method, the tool variable method, the breakpoint regression, etc. The main way to learn is to read the latest empirical articles in the top economic journals and to copy the results with the program. The course will learn how to use the most appropriate causal identification methods, depending on the different research scenarios, different data structures. The second objective of the course is to build capacity for front-line research in development economics. The course is intended to select a large number of empirical articles from other developing countries and to cover major topics of economic development, with the aim of developing an international perspective of students for research and gaining insight into China ' s economic problems from the economic development of other countries. The course requires students to learn to identify gaps and shortcomings in existing literature and to conduct their own original research. The main way to do this is to read the existing literature from a critical point of view and submit its own research plans at the end of the school year. This course is intended for doctoral students in the second grade and above, and for students who are highly qualified. The first course requirement is the first year of a doctorate in economics. Student and undergraduate students who are particularly interested in causal identification methods are also welcome.

Name: Analysis in the New Political Economy
Introduction: The Secretary-General of Xi stated on 17 May 2016 at a workshop on the theoretical work of philosophy and social sciences: “We should have the most say in the interpretation of Chinese practice and in the construction of Chinese theory, but in fact our philosophy and social sciences are less vocal at the international level and are in a situation where there is no reason to speak or speak. Guided by Marxist politico-economics, the course correctly understands the contradictions between “productivity and productive relations”, “economic fundamentals and upper-level architecture” by leading students to the classics of new politico-economics. The purpose of this course is to teach students how to properly use the analytical methods of the new political economy to understand the rapid growth of the Chinese economy over the past 40 years, to summarize the experiences that have led to the success of the Chinese economy and to rise to theory, and to produce high-quality academic papers. In addition to requiring selected students to report classic papers on new political economics in the classroom, the curriculum requires the selected students to submit a semester paper after the end of the term. The course is divided into theoretical and Chinese studies, the theoretical part studies classic theoretical literature on new political economics, and the Chinese research part studies the latest papers on Chinese political economics. Theoretically speaking, Zhang Peng Fei and Chinese research by Yoo Yang.

Name: International Financial Institutions and Global Financial Governance
Introduction:
Through classroom teaching, case analysis, interactive exchange, literature reading and thematic studies, in the context of the development of the global financial governance architecture, systematic presentation of the roles and functions of international financial organizations, as well as the practices and challenges of China ' s participation in the operations of international financial organizations and global financial governance, to help students gain insight into the latest developments in the practice of international financial organizations and the evolution of global financial governance, and to develop internationalized thinking and capacity.
Teachers are experts from national ministries with extensive experience in foreign affairs, mostly in senior positions in international financial organizations. Based on a comprehensive presentation of the global financial governance framework, the instructors will focus on key international (regional) financial organizations such as the World Bank (WB), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS), the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIID), financial standard-setting bodies, the functions, structures, business models of multilateral financial development agencies and our country ' s participation in the operations of these international organizations, taking into account its own expertise and experience. In addition, a work-sharing meeting of international organizations was organized to invite staff of international organizations to share experiences and interact.
Students are required to improve their reading of the literature in conjunction with the content of the lectures, to identify selected topics at the end of the period, to complete written personal studies and to participate in the panel ' s defence.

Name: Topics in International Finance
Introduction: Course Introduction Economic globalization affects many aspects of a country or region. The implications of economic globalization, in particular international financial integration, for the financial markets, economic development and macroeconomic policies of developing countries are important lessons for China ' s participation in international markets. The course will explore capital markets, macroeconomics and related economic policies from a global perspective. Specifically, the course is an optional specialized course for second-grade or higher-grade graduate students on the empirical and theoretical frontier issues of international finance and international macroeconomics. The course is divided into two parts: the first part presents empirical research on financial markets and economic cycles in an international perspective and explores relevant qualitative and quantitative analytical tools. The second part learns how to apply these tools to specific international financial and macroeconomic issues. The curriculum will be as follows: basic models of macroeconomic analysis in an open economy; macroeconomic dilemmas in an open economy; real economic cycles — data and models; random trends in economic cycles; cross-border risk sharing and synchronized adjustment; financial crisis and capital controls; sovereign debt — risks, defaults and spreads; medium- and long-term effects of financial crises; capital flows and global imbalances; and exchange and monetary policy. The courses are advanced macroeconomics, advanced microeconomics and advanced econometrics. Post-school work may be submitted in group form, but not in more than two persons per group. What? Bibliography Review (10%): This course does not have an in-class intermediate examination, but an unpublished paper is selected for evaluation. The reporting period is 20 minutes each. Other students need to be actively involved in the discussions.

Name: European Economic History
Introduction: The aim of this course is to study and explore the evolution of economic development in Europe from multiple angles and levels, and to use this as a basis for exploring the nature of economic problems in China, leading students to master the main theories of development economics and deepening their understanding of our economy.

Name: Quantitative Macroeconomics
Introduction:
I. Course DescriptionThe objective of this course is to introduce graduate students to numerical methods and their computer implementations for solving economic models. Models in modern macroeconomics often are analytically intractable and have no closed-form solutions. In order to answer many interesting questions in the field, macroeconomists have been leaning more and more on numerical solutions of their models using powerful computers. In this course, we will learn many of the standard computational techniques required to solve such models. We will study computational methods that have seen many applications in economics and policy analysis. The economic applications will cover a wide range of problems including models from finance, macroeconomics, industrial organization and other research areas.

We begin by a brief survey of numerical methods required when analytical methods are not available for solving equations and systems of equations, for finding derivatives and integrals, and for solving optimization problems. After this, in the context of some standard representative agent dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models, we will look at methods that can be used to solve them, including value function iteration, policy function approximation, parameterized expectation algorithm, projection method and perturbation.

Name: Topics in Monetary Policy and Financial Stability
Introduction:
Various transactions in the economy are linked to currency and monetary policy affects all aspects of economic activity. The supply of money, interest rates, exchange rates, statutory deposit reserves, etc. affect in different ways the supply of labour, the portfolio of assets, and the production and investment decisions of enterprises. However, the onset of the global financial crisis and the response of many central banks have shown some limitations of monetary policy. In the aftermath of the crisis, central banks, including the People ' s Bank, in many countries adopted a different degree of policy mix combining monetary and macroprudential policies. A number of scholars have also successively proposed new research approaches to the challenges of monetary policy.
This postgraduate course focuses on monetary policy and macroprudential policy and is primarily teaching. The details include two parts. The first part details the new Keynes macroeconomics and how the new Keynes framework is used to analyse monetary policy. The second part, based on financial intermediaries such as banks and financial markets, describes how the global financial crisis and its consequences are understood and then analyses how the new Keynesian framework is used to analyse financial friction and monetary and macroprudential policies. Finally, we discuss our monetary policy and macroprudential policy.

Name: Productivity Theory and Macroeconomic Measurement
Introduction: Within the framework of the neoclassical concept of economic growth, the course is based on productivity theory, with China ' s macroeconomic data as an example, leading the graduate economics system to learn the theory and methodology for measuring output, prices, capital and labour inputs, and to enhance understanding of China ' s evidence of long-term economic growth and productivity performance. The establishment of this course has benefited from the teaching of long-term research and teaching experience in relevant fields, aimed at filling an important gap in the curriculum of the National Graduate School of Economics. This course requires students to have a good basis for macroeconomic theory and its micro-base, as well as some logical understanding of macroeconomic data. The course also requires students to have an independent reading ability in English and an independent reading of the theory, empirical evidence and measurement models in the literature. The teaching methods are guided by modular themes (including partial instruction in English), literature reading under the curriculum, discussion of reports in the course, and the writing of semester papers. There are no classroom examinations, and student performance is assessed for quality in reading reports, classroom discussions and semester papers.

Name: Topics in Macroeconomics and Monetary Economics
Introduction: It is a research course in macroeconomics for higher-level graduate students, with monetary economics as the main element. This course has two objectives. The first is the teaching of important issues and methods now in macro-currency economics. The second is to build the capacity of students to conduct high-quality research independently. After teaching the foundations of monetary economics, students are led to study topics that are now at the forefront of research. Monetary economics is a discipline of great theoretical and empirical development in macroeconomics. The course has thus helped students to improve their ability to conduct theoretical, empirical and quantitative research and to learn the most common methods. Specifically, classic models of new Keynes economics, empirical evidence of wage and price glue, fixed adjustment cost models, information friction, financial friction, optimal monetary policy, networking and heterogeneity are taught.

Name: Urban and Regional Economics
Introduction: This course is intended for doctoral students in the second grade and above, and for students who are highly qualified. The first course requirement is the first year of a doctorate in economics. Selected subjects are also welcomed by master ' s and undergraduate students who are particularly interested in urban and regional economics. The main objective of the course is to build capacity to produce cutting-edge studies on urban and regional economics, particularly from the perspective of new structural economics. The content and mandate of the course are structured around two dimensions. One is familiar with the main concepts, ideas and models in this field. The main methods are classroom instruction, reading of papers under the curriculum and completion of the subject. On the other hand, the course requires students to learn to look for gaps and shortcomings in existing literature and to carry out their own original research. The main way to do this is to read the existing literature from a critical point of view and submit its own research plans at the end of the school year.

Name: Topics in Advanced Econometrics
Introduction: The course is intended to introduce four topics of advanced econometrics: measurement modelling of financial volatility and risk; data mining; machine learning methods and evidence for text-based large data analysis; and non-participatory model estimates. At the end of the course, students should have the appropriate basic models, analytical methods, and be able to complete their studies on each subject through a process of writing, using these methods in their own empirical research.

Name: Empirical Industrial Organization
Introduction:
Industrial organizations mainly study market structures, corporate competition behaviour and consumer demand. Relevant policy issues include anti-monopoly competition, consumer protection, product pricing and positioning, and company merger analysis.
This post-graduate course is devoted to structural measurement estimation models commonly used in research by industry organizations to broaden the scope of research by students in evidence-based economic studies. This course has a high demand for econometric foundations. The content of the course is delivered mainly in the form of essays and practical exercises. The details include three parts. The first part describes in detail the estimates of consumer demand models, including the simple discrete selection model and the random coefficient discrete selection model, as well as the application of such models in industrial organizations and other areas of economics. Part II focuses on market entry models and applications for static enterprises. Part III briefly describes individual dynamic models and related applications.

Name: Fundamentals of Strategic Management
Introduction:
This course offers a comprehensive survey of contemporary strategic management literature, covering those milestone classics, fundamental research topics, as well as major theoretical perspectives. It addresses both strategy content and process issues and reviews both conceptual works and empirical studies.
The course is intended primarily for doctoral students or advanced master's students who expect to conduct research in strategic management or related areas (e.g., organizational behavior, marketing strategy, corporate finance, industrial organization, sociology of organizations, organization theory, or complex decision making).
Each week we will examine a major topic in strategic management. Our approach will typically involve reading the seminal works (or recent summaries or syntheses) on the topic and examining in depth three or four articles. Further readings are suggested for interested students to explore the topic in more depth.
Course Requirements
This course is organized as a seminar, which means that each and every student is required to read, prepare, present, and discuss the required readings. The students should be able to intelligently critique the articles assigned, to find potential linkages among the different articles, discover possible patterns emerged from a set of readings, or identify theoretical gaps as well as methodological deficiencies in the readings. Class participation and contribution are an important and indispensable part of the course for each student. It counts for 50% of a student's final course grade.
At the end of the semester, each student will write a fully-developed research proposal dealing with a topic in the strategy field, and present it to the full class in the last class period. The proposal is expected to include 1) conceptual background, 2) theory development and hypotheses, and 3) methodology. The proposal should clearly specify the potential contribution it makes to the literature. The research proposal and its presentation account for 50% of a student's final course grade.

Name: Innovation and Entrepreneurship
Introduction:
Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying opportunities, acquiring and organizing the resources needed, while at the same time taking the risks and returns associated with the new business. Entrepreneurial activity is considered a key driver of technological development and economic growth.
In a truly multidisciplinary field of research, entrepreneurship integrates economics, management, sociology, psychology and other disciplines. Three facts illustrate its position at the forefront of management research. First, innovation and entrepreneurship were highlighted as engines of future economic growth at the national and global levels, respectively. Second, over 80 per cent of universities offer entrepreneurship courses and over 100 research centres focus on entrepreneurship research in the United States. Finally, not only is there a rapid increase in the number of teaching staff in this field, but there is also a growing demand for research in this field.
This course is different from other courses. First, we will present the classic and current research on innovation and entrepreneurship, which will provide you with a quick and basic understanding of this important and emerging area. Second, students will have the opportunity to engage in academic and field research for genuine start-ups. Finally, company cases will be combined with research papers to better link theory to practice.

Name: Topics in Consumer Behavior: Choice and Judgment
Introduction: The purpose of this seminar is to provide selective coverage of the research carried out in the area of judgment and decision making. We will focus on the theories relevant to understanding how people make choices in a variety of settings. For each topic, we will attempt to determine the main ideas and research issues which have driven work in that area; what we have learned to date; and what gaps exist in our knowledge. Class discussion will include conceptual topics, which deal with substantive issues in the domain of judgment and decision behavior, and research methodologies, which involve a discussion of the process of generating academic research. Coursework consists of scholarly readings, class presentations, and a term paper (research proposal).

Name: Thesis Writing in Management
Introduction: The writing of dissertations is an essential part of academic research and a difficult part of academic research. The purpose of this course is to provide graduate students with guidance on the writing of papers in the field of management, including the selection of the subject and foreword, the methodology of the literature review, the main points of academic writing, the contribution of the papers and the revision process.

Name: Research Methods in Psychology
Introduction:
The curriculum consists of two parts: theoretical courses and a small number of experimental courses.
The purpose of the course is to acquire the basic paradigms and methods of psychological fundamentals and psychological research, to lay the foundation for students to read psycho-scientific papers and conduct future scientific experimental research on their own; and to equip students with the capacity to independently design psychological experiments and analyse research results through the study of psychological theory and experiments. The content of the curriculum therefore focuses on the experimental procedures of the classic experiments, not only on the main results of the psychological process studies, but also on how they were extracted from the experiments.
Students are advised to learn their own basics of General Psychology before attending classes.

Name: Topics in Social Cognition: Human Attachment
College: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
Introduction: This course focuses on topics related to attachment in the field of social cognitive research. Systematic analysis of human attachment will be carried out from a psychological perspective. It is based mainly on the theory of attachment, a comprehensive presentation of the origins and manifestations of love. The main elements will include: the evolution of attachment from an evolutionary perspective; the attachment of children and their individual differences; the attachment of adolescents and their influence factors; the formation and measurement of adult attachment; and recent developments in the theory of attachment. In this course, a more systematic and comprehensive presentation of the theory of attachment will be carried out through multidisciplinary research. Name: Social Stratification and Mobility
Introduction: The purpose of this course is to help graduate and doctoral students to systematically reflect and study issues related to social stratification, mobility and inequality. The curriculum takes into account general theory, methodology, discovery and Chinese social characteristics, and focuses on frontier studies on social stratification, mobility and inequality in sociology, economics and other social sciences.

Name: Topics in Gender and Family
Introduction: Gender is an important factor in social stratification and inequality, and the family is the most central and fundamental unit of society. The purpose of this course is to familiarize students with issues related to gender and the family through the introduction of classical theory and empirical research, which will help them to better understand the economic, political and cultural mechanisms of society. In addition, the course will develop students ' writing skills in English and their ability to think independently, laying the foundation for future academic research.

Name: Marketing Models I
Introduction: The main objective of the course was to understand and build marketing models by introducing various research methods. Students need to have basic statistical, econometric and microeconomic foundations before attending the course. Teaching requirements include: (1) Teaching and reading of classic literature by teachers, making students aware of consumer selection models, new product diffusion models, joint analysis models, Bayesian methods, survival analyses, customer life value models, etc. (2) The introduction of software commonly used for the analysis of several marketing models, such as Matlab, R, SAS, Winbugs, and the gradual familiarization of students with one or several major programming software through post-school exercises. The main references are articles published in leading international academic journals. The course also discusses the direction of outreach research related to each subject.

Name: Marketing Models II
Introduction: This course focuses on the modeling approach from other disciplines to understanding marketing phenomena and facilitating marketing decision making. As such, it is an advanced view of marketing, stressing mathematical and analytical models that have been developed in other areas to analyze marketing problems and phenomena. The topics mainly include social networks methodology from sociology, the event study methodology from finance and their applications in marketing.

Name: Philosophy of Education
Introduction: Higher education has traditionally been an area closely linked to philosophy. Philosophy has been a core subject at medieval universities and recent universities, where the philosophy and philosophy were inextricably linked to reality. Since the twentieth century, the importance of higher education in national and social life has become increasingly prominent, and the philosophy of higher education as a discipline has evolved from independence to maturity. In keeping with the fundamental principles of logical and historical unity, this course offers a more comprehensive overview and summary of philosophical issues that exist in the history and reality of higher education, and explores the possibility of establishing an indigenous Chinese philosophy of higher education, taking into account the actual situation of higher education in the country. While seeking to have a solid theoretical basis, the course has brought together some of the ideas and ideas that I have developed in recent years with regard to philosophical research in higher education. It is also intended to share some of the more novel and unique elements that will, in the belief, be useful for the selection of topics and theoretical research in higher education and other related specializations. This course, which is part of the Educational Philosophy Study series, requires the choice of subjects to have the basis for the subject of Educational Philosophy. In addition, it requires learners to have a knowledge background in higher education research, and it is desirable to integrate curriculum learning organically with graduate papers. Appendix: Curriculum: Module I: Conceptual analysis of higher education: 1) China's ancient theory of advanced knowledge; 2) The idea of university education in ancient India and Arab regions: 3) The Middle Age University concept; 4) The recent concept of Western universities; Module II: Philosophy issues in modern higher education: 1) philosophies in higher education policy - The philosophy of higher education in Brubeck; 2) The critical aspect of modern higher education - higher education in the context of neo-Marxism; 3) The restructuring of modern higher education - higher education in post-modern discourse; (4) Multicultural participation - the way forward in the philosophy of higher education; Module III: Research paradigm for modern higher education: 1) The rationalist paradigm; 2) Pragmatism: 3) Structural functionalist paradigm: 4) Marxist paradigm; Module IV: Building a Chinese philosophy of higher education: 1) The knowledge doctrine - the cultural foundation of Chinese theory of higher education; 2) The law on material evidence - the soul of higher education reform in China; 3) Intellectual responsibilities and obligations - Key factors for success or failure in higher education in China: 4) The confrontation between school culture and popular culture - the state of higher education in China;

Name: Process and Methods of Educational Research
Introduction: Aims of teaching: The purpose of this course is to provide the language, principles, reasoning and methods of conducting empirical research on education, so that students can understand and master the process, logic and basic methods of conducting empirical research on education. Forms of teaching: a combination of classroom lectures, student group discussions, student classroom reports and class discussions. Each student needs to combine a study to practice the basic steps of the research process. Target audience: M.A. and Ph.D., Faculty of Education. Name: Studies in the Localization of Chinese Educational Philosophy
Introduction:
One of the outstanding problems in the field of education theory today is the influx of various "advanced" theories from abroad, which is more prevalent among national scholars. In fact, looking at China's history of educational theory for more than a hundred years at a macro level, we can find a more clear line of theoretical choice for "Practicalism-Marxism-Scientificism-post-modernism". Outside the country, these philosophies are almost intertemporal; in our country, they display logical and time-consuming features. This reminds us that the dissemination of Western educational theory in our country is not disorderly, but has the inevitability of steps and processes that combine Chinese culture and national circumstances. Under the title of "Research on the localization of Chinese educational philosophy", Hetu explains this inevitability with the students and is thus able to meet the challenges of Western theory in a proactive theoretical manner.
This course is part of the "Physical Studies in Education" course series, which requires students attending classes to have a "Pedagogical Philosophy" learning base. Name: The University and Knowledge: A Sociology of Science Perspective
Introduction:
Scientific sociology has always regarded the issue of higher education fields as an important research orientation, producing a large number of research findings that can be drawn upon by higher education researchers. Burton Clark, an American leading scholar in higher education research, recalled that scientific sociology should be an area of focus for higher education researchers.
However, higher education researchers have not paid enough attention to the literature on the sociology of science and its related fields (scientific history, science and technology policy). The purpose of this course is to introduce the basic theory of science sociology, the basic research paradigm, and research in science sociology in the fields of academic history, academic evaluation, academic profession, academic ethics, university-industry relations, etc. The purpose of the curriculum: Higher education research has traditionally been dominated by the dichotomy between teaching and research, with little attention paid to research activities in higher education. This course seeks to familiarize students with the basic theories and methods of science sociology, science and technology policy and to improve their capacity to analyse higher education issues by systematically reading the literature of relevant scholars on higher education research, understanding scientific activities and the impact of science and technology policy on the higher education system.

Introduction: With the widespread use of information and communication technology (ICT) in universities, the use of the Internet for the organization and implementation of teaching activities has become a common development in the educational reform of universities in various countries, of which E-Learning is a representative. At present, many studies show that teachers ' knowledge and mastery of E-Learning ' s basic design and application methods, both at home and abroad, have become one of the key teaching skills that information age teachers cannot ignore. In a broad sense, it is generally accepted that all forms of learning that are implemented using scientific and technological tools (art. Technology-based learning, which is considered to be E-Learing (ASD, 2007). In the narrowest sense, E-Learning refers to a new model of teaching and organizing, organizing, transmitting and managing teaching/training processes, mainly in combination with and using various Internet technologies. Its content consists mainly of the transfer of teaching content in multiple formats (delivery), the management of learning processes and experiences, the establishment of "learning communities" where learners communicate with each other, and the design and development of digital content. The main purpose of this course is to familiarize the Ph.D./Masters of the Institute of Education with this important development in the reform of teaching at the national and international institutions of higher education, so that they can understand the concepts, types and characteristics of E-Learning. At the same time, hands-on exercises and exercises have enabled students to acquire initial knowledge of the characteristics, design strategies and operational methods of the various E-Learning technology platforms. In general, after this course, students will be given the basic skills to design, organize and implement the curriculum using the E-Learning approach. To give them full experience of the revolutionary changes in the way they teach and learn in the information age, laying the foundation for a future teaching career. Although the curriculum is offered by teachers of the Faculty of Education and Technology, there are no special skill requirements for elective students. Students with basic information skills such as computer-based text-processing, e-mail and web browsing, whether in higher education or in the educational economy, may take this course. As computer software designs develop graphically, the operational interface becomes more friendly and the skill requirements for users are reduced accordingly. For the implementation of E-Learning, the design, organization and management of the course are more important elements in the implementation process. Specific operations have become easy for anyone with basic information. One point to be made is that students wishing to take this course should preferably have their own computer and have access to the Internet. Name: Economics of Higher Education
Introduction:
The course is a thematic discussion (optional) course for Master ' s and PhD students in economics and management. Through classroom discussions and independent research, the course will inform students about cutting-edge issues in the economics of higher education and develop academic research capacity. This course requires students to have basic knowledge of basic statistical and quantitative research methods and educational economics.

Name: Quantitative Evaluation Methods for Education Programs
Introduction:
The project evaluation refers to a systematic study of the effectiveness of a policy project using social research methods. This may include the stage of conception and formulation of social projects, to the process of implementation and management, as well as the evaluation of their results and efficiency. While the course will also involve project development and implementation, the main objective is to teach students how to use econometric methods and data to empirically test the effectiveness of a project or policy.

Introduction:

Name: Foundations of Higher Education Management Research: A Sociological Perspective
Introduction: Purpose of the course: (1) The core areas of education management research are education organization, education system, education administration and education policy. There is a close link between education organizations, the education system, education administration and educational policy, which is often overlooked as courses move into depth and specialization, making the phenomenon of education management less holistic. In view of this, the curriculum provides a platform for integrating the basics of education management, corresponding to the topic of educational organization, system and policy research, which is a high-level curriculum, and it is hoped that some improvements will be made to the system-building of education management curricula. (2) This course will provide a more comprehensive introduction to the basic social sciences on which educational management institutes rely, such as sociology, anthropology, political science, etc. As an introductory course in educational management studies, the curriculum will also provide a comprehensive introduction to the general theory and methodology of education management and provide a good basis for students to enter sub-field research, such as organizational theory, institutional theory and policy theory. (3) The course takes an organizational sociological perspective and focuses on how the organization is formed and organized and how it works. The constituent elements of the organization are derived from the social system in which it operates, and it is necessary to examine its formation and functioning in relation to the social environment in which it operates. This is the main tenet of sociology in education, as well as in the organization of sociology, and this course seeks to clarify this issue. The curriculum is therefore theoretical in nature and is not about the basic profile, basic content of school organization and education administration, but about how to understand and study school organization and education administration. (4) The course focuses on the interaction between the two subjects, promoting the research orientation of actions and processes, and organizing the content with higher education as the subject, with due regard to basic education. (5) This course seeks to familiarize students with basic theory, basic educational management facts, familiarity with basic research materials and the ability to master basic research and educational management phenomena. The curriculum will be developed on a theoretical basis, highlighting case studies and covering basic aspects of education management. Examination methods: The course is taught in the form of a combination of teaching by teachers and extra-curricular reading and classroom discussions, and is examined in the form of an intermediate paper for the semester and a course paper, in the form of "three": an article to be read in the classroom (20 points), an overview of the literature to be completed in a certain area during the course of study or a review of a related monograph (40 points), an article to be written at the end of the course to address a relevant reality (40 points).
