Name: Environmental Interface Chemistry
College: College of Urban and Environmental Sciences
Introduction: The multi-media interface process for contaminants determines their transport transformation and biological effects, revealing the control mechanisms of the interface process as a prerequisite for the development of new materials and methods for pollution control/remediation. This course addresses important processes such as adsorption - desorption, hydrolysis and oxidation - on the surfaces of various media for contaminants (heavy metals, persistent organic pollutants and new organic pollutants) in the aquatic environment, revealing patterns of pollutant and environmental media performance and decomposing key factors for controlling environmental behaviour and biological effects of pollutants.

Name: Environmental Monitoring Technology
College: College of Urban and Environmental Sciences
Introduction: Environmental monitoring technology is a basic technical means in environmental research. It mainly uses analytical technologies such as sample extraction, purification, and instrumental analysis to efficiently and sensitively separate target pollutants from complex sample media, and conduct an accurate qualitative and quantitative process to provide analytical support for research on the pollution characteristics, migration and transformation behavior of environmental pollutants, and ecological health risks. This course mainly introduces the monitoring technology of major pollutants in environmental media such as water, atmosphere, soil, and solid waste. The main content includes environmental analysis technologies such as extraction, pretreatment and purification, analysis, and biological monitoring of different pollutants in multiple types of samples.

Name: Indoor Air Pollution and Its Control
College: College of Urban and Environmental Sciences
Introduction: Air pollution is one of the primary environmental risks to the health of people and causes premature death. Because the vast majority of the population stays indoors for longer periods of time, indoor air pollution has a significant impact on their respiratory exposure and health hazards. Indoor air pollution and control is a major concern in the field of environmental geosciences. The Indoor Air Pollution and Control course focuses on sources of indoor air pollution, pollution characteristics, basic theories, techniques and methods for indoor pollutant control. Through the course, basic theoretical and technical methods for indoor air pollution control are developed, basic research methods for air pollution health hazards are developed, basic scientific research capabilities for indoor air pollution research and initial case design capabilities for management techniques are developed, basic research capabilities for indoor pollution and its health hazards are developed, and a professional basis for future environmental science and pollution health protection is established.

Name: Numerical Simulation of Air Pollution
College: College of Urban and Environmental Sciences
Introduction:
Numerical pollution modelling and modelling are the main tools and techniques for understanding the physical, chemical processes of atmospheric pollution, quantifying the causes of atmospheric pollution and the pollution-source-sink relationship, predicting the development of atmospheric pollution. They have developed rapidly in recent years, have gained extensive applications in atmospheric pollution research and early warning forecasts, have become indispensable tools and are expected to be developed and applied more rapidly. Air pollution forecasting models cover a wide range of areas of knowledge, including mathematics, atmospheric physics and chemistry, weather climate, and data processing and integration. Through this course, students are initially familiar with and mastered the basic knowledge of numerical patterns of atmospheric pollution, modelling ideas and platforms, and large data processing. Initial knowledge of the operation and use of numerical models of atmospheric pollution through on-board exercises. Through model learning, the theory and knowledge of atmospheric chemistry, physics, the atmospheric environment and the causes of atmospheric pollution are further understood and consolidated.
The course focuses on modelling and control equations for atmospheric pollution patterns, simple numerical methods, atmospheric movements, major atmospheric physics processes for atmospheric pollution, atmospheric boundary layers, chemical processes and mechanisms for atmospheric pollution, and sources and sinks of atmospheric pollution. The course is based on a combination of theoretical learning and on-board practice, with emphasis on the development of modelling skills.

Name: Environmental Laboratory Safety
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction:
Environmental science and engineering is a more practical discipline in which graduate students need to be involved in environmental laboratory experiments and field practices, and the safety of laboratory and field observations is the primary responsibility and necessary knowledge. Environmental-type laboratories have the same safety requirements as traditional chemical laboratories, biological laboratories, physical laboratories, etc., and safety protocols of this specialty, covering both hazardous chemicals, high-temperature and high-pressure facilities, special equipment, and water and electricity, as well as safety matters that require attention, such as biosafety and field practice processes. Experiments therefore need to have solid laboratory and field safety knowledge and skills.
The teaching of environmental laboratory safety covers laboratory safety facilities, fire safety, pressure container safety, water electrical safety, disposal of hazardous chemicals and waste, radiation and radiation safety, biosafety, safety of field practice, etc., by focusing on safety examples in specialized and relevant experimental types, by means of lectures by teachers, on-site visits and hands-on exercises, leading students to safety awareness and responsibility, learning safety knowledge, training safety skills, developing safety habits to guide students to safety awareness and responsibilities, learning safety knowledge, training safety skills and developing safety habits.

Name: Environmental Issues and Management of Chemical Substances
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: While the development and application of chemicals provide a wide range of well-being and convenience to human society, as the environment and life sciences progress, chemicals are increasingly being exposed to potentially toxic effects on the ecological environment and human health, and chemical environmental problems are evolving into global public risks and environmental safety crises. The environmentally sound management of chemicals has been identified as an important component of the global sustainable development strategy, and since the twenty-first century, environmental management of chemicals has emerged as an important agenda for environmental protection in the world today. The postgraduate course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of chemicals and their hazards (GHS), potential environmental and health risks and the corresponding scientific and management implications, familiarization with the underlying principles and methods of chemical hazard assessment, risk assessment and risk management, systematic analysis and understanding of the basics of chemicals environmental management and existing underlying systems, and understanding and exploration of environmental management practices for both intermediate and foreign chemicals. Courses will be taught in conjunction with existing chemical substance risk assessment cases and international conventions such as POPs, EDCs or other topics of high international concern (SVHCs). The course is a specialized course in the frontier and emerging exploratory fields of environmental science and management in the country and is available for postgraduate studies in environmental science and environmental management and related professions.

The purpose of the course is to help graduate students acquire basic theories and methodologies for atmospheric chemistry modelling, to understand today ' s atmospheric chemistry models and their development, and to build the capacity of students to apply numerical modelling methods to atmospheric environmental studies. The course focuses on the principles, methods and applications of the main models commonly used in atmospheric chemistry modelling studies, including box models, trajectories, photochemical oxidation models, acid deposition models, aerosol models, integrated air quality models, and pollution source emission modelling and application of models.

Name: Pollution Meteorology

Principles of meteorology, particularly these of boundary-layer meteorology, micrometeorology and atmospheric turbulence, are briefly introduced. Relevant theoretical treatment and method are used to deal with air pollutant transport, diffusion and removing. Students can use what they learn in this course to applications such as environmental assessment, air pollution control and environmental planning etc. Four parts are introduced in this course:
1)Fundamentals of meteorology and atmospheric boundary layer theory.
2)Theory and application of atmospheric diffusion. Majorly on turbulent dispersion theory, result, application limit, and simple models.
3)Processes that influence the air pollutant dispersion, including near-source processes, deposition, boundary layer height and complex terrain, and their treatment in models.
4)Research development in atmospheric environment problems and meteorological influence in these problem.

Name: Optical Measurement Techniques for Air Pollution
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: At present, atmospheric pollution in our country has become a matter of widespread public and international concern. The solution to the problem of atmospheric pollution needs to be based on a clear understanding of the mechanisms by which atmospheric pollution is formed, while high-precision online measurements of atmospheric compositions (free radicals, gaseous pollutants, aerosols) are key to in-depth research into the causes of atmospheric pollution. Optical methods are based on measurements of the optical properties of species (photo-absorption and dispersion) in order to quantify their atmospheric concentrations. They are characterized by high measurements of accuracy, short response times and low maintenance levels and are applicable to online monitoring of multiple key atmospheric pollutants. With the rapid development of optical technologies and components such as lasers, photovoltaic diodes and CCD detection, optical measurement techniques are increasingly being used in atmospheric pollution monitoring and scientific research. The Academy of Environmental Sciences and Engineering, which is the national centre of excellence for atmospheric pollution research, has over the past decade used a great deal of optical measurement techniques in laboratory and off-site observation research and has accumulated extensive experience in technological research and development and applications. Schoolteachers have long been involved in research on mechanisms for the formation of atmospheric pollution, which involves the use and development of a wide range of advanced optical measurement techniques, including spectral radiometers, differential optical absorption spectrum, cavity enhancement absorption spectrum, laser induction fluorescent, and in-depth and comprehensive knowledge of optical measurement techniques for atmospheric pollution. In view of the current high demand for optical measurement techniques and the lack of relevant content systems for teaching, it is proposed to apply for a course on Optical Measurement of Atmospheric Pollution. The course is offered to graduate students and is taught in multimedia teaching. The courses focused on the basic principles of optical techniques for measuring atmospheric trace composition, instrument design and applications in atmospheric pollution monitoring and theoretical research. The main features of the course are based on a study of the working principles and applications of existing advanced optical instruments, an in-depth study of the underlying theoretical and applied elements of optical measurement techniques for atmospheric pollution and an understanding of their trends, with a view to operationalizing theoretical learning to support the successful development of research related to atmospheric pollution research. Through this course, students can acquire basic knowledge and basic theory of the optical properties of atmospheric pollutants and trace components, gain insight into key elements such as design thinking, working principles, application difficulties, data analysis, etc. of optical measuring instruments, and provide a solid foundation for better use and design of new instruments. Through learning, students are able to fully understand the whole process of a optical measurement instrument from its principles, design, set-up and application. At the end of the course, students are able to design simple and innovative measurement instruments based on practical needs and principles.

Name: Kinetics of Atmospheric Chemical Reactions
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: Atmospheric chemical reaction dynamics are the science of studying patterns of chemical transformation of trace inorganic and organic substances in the atmosphere and are the most important theoretical basis for atmospheric chemistry. Its specific task is to study quantitatively the chemical reaction rates of these substances in the atmosphere, to reveal the response mechanisms, to assess their atmospheric fate and the effects of climate change on the environment and climate. The purpose of this course is to provide students with basic theoretical knowledge in this area. The course will include: 1 introductory statement; 2 fundamentals of chemical reaction dynamics; 3 atmospheric photochemistry base; 4 atmospheric resonance; 5 atmospheric inequity and multi-comparison; 6 atmospheric response laboratory simulation techniques; 7 typical atmospheric pollution event causal analysis; 8 field observation data dynamics analysis; and 9 atmospheric reactions and climate change interactions.

Name: Frontier Discussion on Volatile Organic Compounds and Compound Air Pollution
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction:
At present, atmospheric pollution in our country has become a matter of widespread public and international concern, and atmospheric pollution presents a composite pollution characteristic of both particulate matter and ozone pollution. Volatile organic matter is a key species in the process of “formation-evolution-dispersion” of composite atmospheric pollution, and a comprehensive understanding of the sources, transformation, removal, etc. of volatile organic matter is the basis for an in-depth understanding of mechanisms for the formation of composite atmospheric pollution. The Academy of Environmental Sciences and Engineering is the national leader in conducting integrated atmospheric pollution research and is a national leader in the online measurement of volatile organic matter, in sinks and in chemical conversion mechanisms. Schoolteachers have a long history of research on volatile organic matter ' s transformational degradation mechanisms, involving online measurements of volatile organic matter, chemical reaction mechanisms, integrated field observations and systematic understanding of the interaction of volatile organic matter with atmospheric composite pollution. In the light of the increasing emphasis on volatile organic matter in the country and the lack of relevant courses dedicated to the advancement of volatile organic matter in our home, it is proposed to apply for a course entitled " Frontline discussion on volatile organic matter and atmospheric composite pollution " .
The course is offered to postgraduate students. The courses focused on high-precision measurement techniques for volatile organic matter, source resolution, chemical transformation mechanisms, and the role of atmospheric particulate matter and ozone generation. The main features of the course are in the form of discussion sessions, which systematically review and streamline the progress of research on volatile organic matter at home and abroad, recognize its lack of research, and look ahead to the direction of subsequent research, provide an in-depth overview of the contribution of volatile organic matter emissions and chemical transformation to atmospheric composite pollution, and support the successful development of research related to atmospheric pollution research through classroom learning and discussion.

Name: Environmental Economics
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: The course is a postgraduate research programme to raise awareness of important theoretical and academic issues through classical literature and up-to-date academic frontier literature in the field of student reading, as well as through classroom discussions and seminars, and to enhance students ' ability to use environmental economics expertise for analysis and solutions (policy programmes) through discussion and analysis of important environmental economic policies and socio-environmental-economic issues.

Name: Water Quality Science and Management
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: This course is geared towards a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of water pollution prevention/basin water environment, water ecosystem management policies and frameworks in China, Japan, Europe and the United States, and examines gaps in water environmental management and strategic directions for development in our country. The course included environmental water quality fundamentals, licensing systems and technical principles for control of discharges from sources of water pollution, technical principles for assessment of the environmental quality of watersheds and restoration of damaged water bodies, methods for assessment of the state of aquatic ecosystems and technical principles for restoration, and theory and methodology for control of toxic pollutants. To raise the basic knowledge, raise the level of awareness and competence, broaden the horizon and leadership skills of students who will be engaged in environmental management, scientific research and teaching of water quality and environmental protection, to expand the knowledge of environmental management for students who will be involved in research and development of environmental technology and engineering, and to avoid the misdirected application of engineering technology development. Important knowledge points are as follows: What? Indicators commonly used in pollution control and water quality assessment and their environmental and health implications, including conventional, characteristic, toxic and hazardous pollutant indicators, their values and descriptive benchmarks/criteria; What? The strategic framework structure of the indicator methodology for biological integrity, chemical integrity and physical integrity in assessment of the watershed water environment/water ecosystem quality and integrated multiparametric evaluation; What? (a) A system for the control and licensing of pollution sources, including the formation and core content of regulations for the prevention and control of water pollution in China, Japan, Europe and the United States, pollutant release standards and technical methods for their compliance, and an analysis of the key issues and solutions that the country needs to focus on during the pollution control phase; What? Water environment quality management system. Using the United States Clean Water Act as a case study on maximum daily load plans and technical routes for the screening and restoration of damaged water bodies based on the use of functionally defined water quality evaluation methods and their benchmarks/standards, water quality compliance and their implementation guidelines; What? Integrated water resources and ecosystem management systems. Analysis of the framework structure for integrated management of water resources, water use and water ecosystems, as listed in the EU Water Framework Directive, and examination of ecological conditions assessment, watershed management plans and technical principles for aquatic ecological restoration in the water framework; What? Chemical substances and health: Screening of toxic substances in the aquatic environment, hazard and risk assessment, prioritization and analysis of life-cycle management of industrial chemicals. To examine the progress and cognitive gaps in the international community ' s environmental research on new pollutants of concern, as well as the future vision and strategies of toxic substances management in China. Learning goals are: (1) Deepening the scientific knowledge of environmental water quality and its application in practice, in particular by improving the scientific rationale and application of water quality evaluation indicators and their valuation; (2) Understanding different national pollution source control strategies and their relationship to water environmental management, managing differences in technology-based emission limits and emission limits and portfolio control strategies based on water quality, principles established by national emission standards and licensing systems, selection of key conventional, non-conventional (including nutrient salt) and noxious substance emission control targets and emission compliance modalities; (3) Knowledge of the basic content of management of water quality and problems in the regulatory regime and implementation of management of water quality in China, Japan, the United States and Europe. Types of evaluation and control indicators and the scientific and technical basis for compliance with the three main water service functions of drinking water safety, protection of aquatic organisms and landscape recreation; (4) Understanding the framework structure for synergistic management of water resources and ecosystems, and in-depth examination of relevant indicators for the assessment of the integrity of aquatic ecosystems and their valuation patterns and technical routes for aquatic ecological restoration; (5) Learning from the foundational knowledge of chemical hazards and risk assessment, examining priority assessment, priority management and priority control strategies and major technological pathways in environmental management, and mapping the scientific and technical direction of new attention to environmental management of chemicals in the future water environment. The curriculum is summarized and distributed as follows: 1. Water quality monitoring and evaluation: four school hours; Water quality benchmarks and standards: 4 school hours 3. Pollution source management and licensing system: four school hours; 4. Process-wide control of environmental pollution of industrial chemicals: 4 school hours 5. Environmental quality management of watersheds: four school hours; 6. Drinking water safety assessment: four school hours; 7. Landscape recreational water body management and black water body governance: four school hours; 8. Water quality management and maximum daily load scheme for watershed water: 4 hours 9. Assessment of the integrity of aquatic ecosystems and restoration of aquatic ecosystems: 4 school hours 10. Technical principles of eutrophication processes and control: 4 school hours 11. Chemical hazard and risk assessment strategies and technical routes: 4 school hours 12. Management and pollution control strategies for toxic substances in the aquatic environment: 4 school hours Note: The above is taught by the teacher for three hours in the basics or thematic reports, and one hour in the classroom for pupils. Teaching methods include teaching, research and discussion of studies. Student achievement is assessed as follows: (b) The student classroom discussions and exchanges, as well as the production and presentation of the Pre, where teachers scored 50 per cent of the total; A paper was written on scientific or technical aspects of environmental management of water throughout the curriculum, choosing its own arguments of interest, and teachers rated 50 per cent of the total achievement. If there is a willingness to do so, one-on-one guidance and refinements can fulfil the requirement for input. Schoolteachers choose to meet the requirements for trial and co-sign and recommend to the national core for publication.

Name: Environmental Planning
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction:
The course aims to explore in depth the research content of environmental planning, the research methodology and priority element planning processes, as well as research frontiers and trends at home and abroad. In contrast to the undergraduate environmental planning course, the objectives of the course are to place greater emphasis on developing and directing students to an independent analytical and judgemental capacity based on systematic knowledge and to upgrade the level of research: (1) to focus the course's delivery on the research frontier of environmental planning, research methods and case studies; (2) to highlight the environmental planning “assessment/evaluation, simulation, optimization” and planning decision integration techniques and their application to different elements of environmental planning at national, regional and watershed scales, based on conventional environmental planning research methodologies.
The course provides students with an in-depth knowledge of the basic theory and methodology of environmental planning, as well as of the methodology for the preparation of the various elements of environmental planning, and a systematic understanding of trends and research directions in environmental planning at home and abroad, as well as an improved research capacity and skills for independent research and analysis of environmental planning. They are divided into 10 chapters, namely, basics, planning content, technical methods, water environment planning, atmospheric environmental planning, soil solidity element planning, urban environmental planning, eco-urban planning and watershed environmental planning.

Name: Frontiers of Environmental Management Research
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering

Name: Advanced Lecture Series for Doctoral Students in Physical Geography
College: College of Urban and Environmental Sciences

Name: Theory and Technology of Water Treatment
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction:
The curriculum is guided by fundamental principles, theory and practice, and engineering is applied in a context that focuses on building students ' capacity to analyse and solve problems.
The course presents basic principles and application cases of water treatment technologies, understanding the theoretical and technical research methods, thinking, technical routes, and leading students to cutting-edge scientific issues and technological development hot spots in water treatment.

Name: Global Environmental Problems and Countermeasures
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: The course is aimed at helping students to understand the progress of research and control management in global environmental issues, such as climate change, ozone layer depletion, persistent organic pollutants, mercury, nano and so forth, and at improving the methodological, modelling and policy analysis capabilities of students who are undertaking or interested in studies on global environmental governance.

Name: Compliance Progress and Evaluation
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: The aim of the course is to inform students about the content of the main current international environmental conventions, the objectives of national compliance, the requirements of the conventions for the development of our environmental science; the progress of our compliance, the characteristics of compliance management, the policy needs and systems for compliance; the environmental benefits of compliance and methods of evaluation; and the social and economic impact of compliance actions. The course covers major current global environmental issues, the signing of international environmental conventions, the main objectives and content of the conventions, the obligations of States, China ' s compliance action plan, the economic aspects and challenges of compliance, the establishment of compliance mechanisms, policy systems and measures to ensure compliance, progress and achievements in compliance, and the assessment of the socio-economic and ecological impact of compliance.

Name: Solid Waste Treatment and Disposal
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: Students are equipped with the main technical principles of solid waste disposal and disposal, advances in domestic and foreign technology research, responses to solid waste management and related laws and regulations and standards. Courses on: (1) whole-process management of solid waste generation, collection, transport and disposal, relevant laws and regulations and standards; (2) solid waste incineration and pollution control technologies; (3) biomass composting, biodrying technologies; (4) solid waste landfill treatment and pollution control technologies; (5) solid waste resourceization technologies; (6) new environmental issues and analysis of their responses.

Name: English for Specific Purposes
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction:
The course aims to strengthen the capacity of graduate students to write scientific and technical papers in accordance with the basic requirements for writing international magazine papers. The selection of graduate students for this course requires some research experience, and it is hoped that some basic research findings have been obtained in order to provide basic material for the completion of writing at all stages of the course. The course operation is an important component of the course and reflects its practical and operational nature.
The course consists of two basic phases, the first of which is based on the scientific and technical paper writing experience system, which presents the basic principles of the writing of some papers and the basic elements of each component, from the subject, author, abstract to the introduction, material and methodology, outcome and discussion of the structure of the paper IMRAD. At the same time, a number of relevant experiences and cases in the revision of the papers and responses to the comments of the reviewers were duly discussed.
The second phase consisted of training in academic exchange skills, mainly in the International Moot, which was conducted in English throughout the course of the Conference, from the planning, organization, conference and branch chairs to the writing of conference papers/PPTs, oral reports, discussions and questions by students. Each student is given the same opportunity to report orally at the meeting, and the vast majority of students can participate in the organization and discussion of the meeting.
In addition to pursuing the basic objective of improving students ' writing and academic communication skills, as a direct reflection of the academic achievement of the course, each student hopes to be able to produce an English-language paper at the end of the course based on the various stages of writing.
In principle, the course is not subject to professional restrictions, but is delivered with a focus on environmental science and engineering, water and civil engineering, and geology.

Name: Chemistry of Water Treatment Processes
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: This course, which is one of the basic courses in environmental engineering, focuses on the chemical principles of pollutant management and control processes in water and wastewater. The main elements include the chemical knowledge associated with the more rapidly developing water treatment unit operating processes, such as condensation, advanced oxidation, electrochemical processes, membrane processes, etc. This course provides the theoretical basis for the independent pursuit of scientific research and engineering practices related to water treatment by masters and doctoral students.

Name: Biostatistical Methods and Applications
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: The course is compulsory/optimal for postgraduate students in the field of environmental and health research and may also serve as an optional course for students interested in the field of environmental and health research. The course focused on the basic concepts of the methodology of biological statistics, the use of statistical software and the application of the methodology in environmental health research. The objective of the course is to equip students with the principles, concepts, methods and applications of biostatistics. Through this course, students will be able to identify and describe basic data types; basic calculations of biostatistic variables, including averages, median values, deviations, standard errors, etc.; understanding the links between statistical and hypothetical tests; understanding the nature of Type I and type II error; being able to perform a series of basic hypothetical tests such as t-tests, card-tests, non-parametric tests; understanding and mastering the application of biostatistical methods such as linear regression, logical regression, multiple analysis in physical environmental health research; and skilled statistical software R for statistical analysis of environmental health research data.

Name: Water Environmental Chemistry
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction:
The purpose of this course is to understand the dynamics of aquatic environmental chemistry, to broaden students ' horizons, to broaden research thinking and to really learn to use it.
The main elements include: knowledge of the progress of research on the quality of water in domestic and international rivers, the chemical nature of the main rivers, the characteristics of particulate matter and their impact on water quality; knowledge of the basic characteristics of pollution of heavy metals in rivers, methods of assessment of pollution of heavy metals in sediments, analytical methods and advantages and disadvantages of existing heavy metals in the country and abroad; familiarity with basic principles and methods for the analysis of the sources of lead isotopes; mastering of models and applications for the morphological distribution of natural water-weight metals; understanding of the main organic pollutants in water bodies, their properties and their pAHs; mastering of the transport behaviour, influence factors and hazards to humans of organic pollutants in water bodies; and familiarity with methods for the analysis of domestic and foreign organic pollutants.

Name: Drinking Water Quality Science and Purification Technology
College: College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering
Introduction: (includes the purpose of the course, the basis of the course and the teaching requirements, etc.): The country's main sources of water are contaminated to varying degrees, and the deterioration of drinking water quality will severely constrain the sustained growth of the national economy and seriously affect the safety of drinking water, human health and social stability of the population at large. Safe drinking water purification technologies are one of the effective means of addressing this major problem and have been one of the main directions of environmental science. Starting with the 11th Five-Year Plan, the State has significantly increased its investment in research and engineering in the field of drinking water. The State ' s major demand for drinking water safety requires the training of more specialists in science and purification techniques for drinking water quality. Drinking water quality science, which addresses the relationship between water quality and human health, includes mineral indicators, organic indicators, toxicological indicators, sensory indicators, physical indicators, etc., which are being refined as instruments are analysed, toxicology, hygiene, medicine, etc. Drinking water purification technologies, which address different water quality and treatment requirements, include a variety of individual technologies and combinations of processes such as physics, chemistry, physical chemistry, microbiology, biochemistry, mathematical modelling calculations, chemical engineering, environmental science and environmental engineering, and continue to improve and innovate as various disciplines develop and the new environment is protected. A course entitled " Water quality science and purification techniques " provides students with an overview of drinking water quality science, purification principles and technologies, the latest results and directions of development, and an overview of drinking water purification principles and technical methods, as well as the relationship between water quality and human health. The course shall be an optional postgraduate course in environmental science and environmental engineering and a basic postgraduate course in the direction of water and environment sciences. The curriculum combines the latest advances in drinking water quality science and purification techniques with a view to providing students with a more comprehensive and in-depth understanding of drinking water quality science and purification techniques, a system of indicators of healthy drinking water and active water technologies, treatment of chemical oxidation of drinking water, biotreatment of drinking water, biostability control of drinking water quality, control of drinking water disinfection and by-products of disinfection, control of algae and algae toxins in drinking water, endocrine disruptor control techniques, basic principles and research advances in groundwater purification technologies. In order to better demonstrate the equipment, engineering information involved in drinking water purification technologies and to facilitate student reporting, classrooms are required to have computer projection conditions. Students taking this course should have a more systematic environmental, chemical and biological basis. Learning through this course will lead to a deeper understanding of the science of drinking water quality and the dynamics of clean-up technology development, the key theories of drinking-water purification technologies, and a separate design and analytical capacity for drinking-water purification research and applications.

Name: Design Practice (V): Ecological Planning and Design of Water Systems
College: College of Architecture and Landscape Architecture
Introduction:
This course is a course on eco-design of water systems.
The lecture section includes basic theory and methodology, as well as specific content.
At the heart of this is a planning exercise that combines real projects. All students are required to participate in research and research throughout the project process and to independently complete part of the research and planning elements in the project research and planning process.

Name: Spatiotemporal Intelligence and Smart Cities
College: College of Architecture and Landscape Architecture
Introduction: The ICT technology revolution of recent years has triggered the rapid development of new technologies represented by 5G, IOT, AI, cloud and margin calculations. Geographically, this means that access to big, high-frequency, high-precision time and space data, as well as to the robust communications and computational analysis capabilities required to process those data, is becoming increasingly possible, and that the universal spatial and temporal intelligence that geology and geo-information science has long been apprehensive is becoming a reality. Universal space and time intelligence technology will profoundly reshape the entire urban lifestyle of humankind. This trend is reflected in the “new urban science” proposed by national and international leading scholars, as well as the emergence of intelligent cities around the world. At present, the number of courses offered by our institutions of higher education in the area of space-time intelligence and wisdom in cities is still low, and the number of courses offered is known to be limited in terms of data, methods, applications, etc., and, overall, there is a lack of a complete system to meet the needs of academic development and education. In view of this situation, it is proposed that a course on " Space and Space Smart Cities " be offered at the School of Architecture and Landscape Design at Beijing University. The curriculum will be based on the framework of smart city building, which will systematically introduce data, methods and applications from space and time intelligence to help students develop a comprehensive knowledge map of the relevant areas; at the same time, it will build the capacity of students to apply the knowledge they have learned to solve real wisdom urban problems by analysing real-life research and practical cases, and by independently researching practical ethics for students under the curriculum. The main elements of the course are as follows: What? A city review of space and time intelligence and intelligence; What? New data environment; What? Methods for analysing space and time data: modelling of data, data management and cleansing; construction of space and space field and flow models; space and space model recognition and characterization; space interaction; space and space extrapolation; and visualization of space and space data; What? Time and space intelligence applications: urban planning, urban design, urban governance, urban transport, 2B services, 2C services; What? ICT-supported Universal Time and Space Smart Vision. In parallel, the course consists of a voluntary internship (without merit), which involves training in data analysis techniques and their application. The courses are open elective courses, suitable for subjects such as urban planning, landscape gardening, human geography, geographic information systems, information science, and other doctoral students interested in space-time intelligence and smart cities.

Name: Seminar (VII): Eco-Cities and Ecological Restoration
College: College of Architecture and Landscape Architecture
Introduction:
Aimed at the study of ecological processes and restoration of urbanization,
These include, inter alia, urban water ecosystem processes and regulation; urban water ecological planning and ecological security; and urban ecological restoration and habitat-building.

Name: Design Practice (VII): Rural and Agricultural Landscape Planning and Design
College: College of Architecture and Landscape Architecture
Introduction:
Through theoretical discussions and project-specific planning studies, the course enables students of landscape designers to learn the theory and methodology to understand the mechanisms for the formation of traditional villages and agricultural landscapes in China, the problems encountered in their development, and the prospects for the future, to understand the evolution of rural and agricultural landscapes in China in the broader social, economic and ecological context; to learn about the practical work of the rural and agricultural landscape design industry and to develop the methods and capacities for thinking and addressing rural development issues.
The course combines theoretical teaching, hot-spot lectures and design seminars (Workshop). Students are required to select a theme to present a small paper and to complete a practical case of planning design by clustering or single person for a specific site. The ratio of achievement was 40:60. Thesis is rated by the teacher-in-charge, and the design practice is evaluated and rated by the teacher-in-charge and external experts.

Name: Seminar (I): History and Theory of the Built Environment
College: College of Architecture and Landscape Architecture
Introduction: The course is conducted as a teacher-student one-on-one guide. Teachers guide students in the systematic study of practical scientific issues, and students perform a certain amount of scientific tasks independently of their teachers. Each student is limited to one teacher per semester to direct his or her research and at least one and up to three study series before applying for a degree paper.

Name: Whitehead and the Book of Changes
Introduction: The pre-Dalvin dominant narrative of Western philosophy is the pursuit of eternal knowledge, and Darwin's rejection of the concept of “species” challenges this. The White Sea was the first “process thinker” to seek knowledge in a world of change. On the other hand, China ' s philosophical narrative began with recognition of the real nature of time and process, as clearly demonstrated by the universal theory of the Easily process. The course will discuss the similarities and differences between the White Sea and Ely. Of course, it's not possible to make a difference.

Name: Chinese Society
Introduction:
This course provides an overview of contemporary China. Chinese society is best understood through a number of different intrinsically-linked and mutually-interdependent aspects. For this reason, we will explore its history, cultural practices, government, economy, and family structure.
Objective: Sociology 428 provides an overview of contemporary China. Chinese society is best understood through a number of different intrinsically-linked and mutually-interdependent aspects. For this reason, we will explore its history, cultural practices, government, economy, and family structure.
Course requirements: All students should meet the following requirements on time. No late work will be accepted, except under extreme circumstances. There will be no incompletes.
1) Students are expected to participate in classroom discussions. Students will be chosen at random to answer questions about assigned readings. They are also encouraged to ask questions during lectures.
2) 3 homework assignments.
3) A mid-term exam will be given. The exam is closed-book.
4) A final term paper is required. The expectation is that you select one of the topics we cover in the class and do additional research on the topic. Develop a theme and find support for the theme.
5) A few films.
Grading: The overall grade will be based on the following components:
Class participation: 10%
Homework Assignments 30% (10% each)
Mid-Term Examination: 30%.
A Research Proposal or the Term Paper: 30%.

Name: China in Transition (Part 1)
Introduction: This yearlong course is a systematic introduction to contemporary China, a revitalizing civilization-state continuously in search of modernity and sustainability against the backdrop of globalization. By focusing on China’s transition to the Reform era in the recent three decades, this course is intended (1) to familiarize students with different perspectives on China’s ongoing transformation and future trends centered on the dual motifs of modernity and sustainability; (2) to offer a close working knowledge of China’s transition in the realms of economy, politics, society, and environment, with a focus on internal dynamics and practices within China – telling real and rich Chinese stories, not a singular “China story”; (3) to engage students in debates on a broad array of issues and topics that bear distinct features, patterns, and even para-doxes of China’s modernization drive through seminars, presentations, and case studies; and (4) to provide students with opportunities of experiential learning by making the best of resources available on the ground in the context of mentor-led case-study research and fieldwork.

Name: Field Research
Introduction:
The purpose of this course is to facilitate students to gain first-hand experience about China’s history and culture as well as contemporary developments.

This course is organized as two one-week trips to different parts of China. All students must participate in both trips. During the trips, professors who lead the trip will organize lectures, discussions, and site visits.

This course offering is arranged to take place in both the fall and the spring semester, but students are registered in the spring semester. Course credits appear in the spring semester of the transcript.

Name: China's Financial System
Introduction: This course is a survey of China's financial system, including its banking industry, monetary policy structure, and financial markets (bonds, derivatives, equities, foreign exchange, alternative asset management, and related markets). The goal is an integrated view of how capital, risk, and liquidity are intermediated within China and cross-border. Current trends (including liberalization of markets) will be emphasized. Coverage will be through lectures, reading of both primary source documents and secondary (journalistic and analyst) commentary, as well as a range of subject-matter-expert speakers. Using our special High Immersion Classrooms at Stanford and at the Stanford Center at PKU, this course meets jointly with a parallel course offered at Beijing University. Students will participate actively in class discussion, make a 5-minute topical presentation, and submit a short (10-page) paper.

Name: China in Transition (Part 2)
Introduction: This yearlong course is a systematic introduction to contemporary China, a re-vitalizing civilization-state continuously in search of modernity and sustaina-bility against the backdrop of globalization. By focusing on China’s transition during the Reform era in the recent three decades, this course is intended (1) to familiarize students with different perspectives on China’s ongoing trans-formation and future trends centered on the dual motifs of modernity and sustainability; (2) to offer a close working knowledge of China’s transition in the realms of economy, politics, society, and environment, with a focus on in-ternal dynamics and practices within China – telling real and rich Chinese sto-ries, not a singular “China story”; (3) to engage students in debates on a broad array of issues and topics that bear distinct features, patterns, and even para-doxes of China’s modernization drive through seminars, presentations, and case studies; and (4) to provide students with opportunities of experiential learning by making the best of resources available on the ground in the context of mentor-led case-study research and fieldwork.

Name: Lecture Series on China Studies
Introduction:
In this China studies lecture series, Yenching Academy will invite scholars from in and outside Peking University to deliver talks on a topic relevant to China. The purpose of this course is to expose students to scholars not involved in YCA teaching to share China insights and opinions. Topics range from history and culture, economic and social development, to sciences in China.

Peking University has many prominent scholars and learning from them benefits students beyond traditional course offerings. Scholars from outside Peking University can complement the strength of PKU faculty.

Ten lectures will be arranged throughout the spring semester. Students need to attend at least seven of them and to turn in a thought piece of no fewer than 2000 words on one of the lectures to get credits. Lectures will be announced one week ahead each time.

Name: Academic Writing
Introduction: Academic Writing is designed to train the students of China studies to have the necessary mindset and skills in writing academic papers and reports in the fields of humanities and social sciences, as well as the proficiency in writing in English. Experts from various disciplines in humanities and social sciences will guide the students to get familiar with the way academic writings are conceptualized, constructed and supported with evidence in their fields.

Name: Chinese Frontier Society: Social and Historical Understanding
Introduction: Frontier society widely exists across the world as a far-flung periphery of a state, a community that acts as a cultural outlier or a human group living at the edge of an ecological system. Frontier societies are commonly seen in the human histories and are known to have created histories of their own. Where are the Chinese frontier societies? What does the frontier society mean to the gigantic space and cultural entity called China in historical times and currently? Who are the social actors in the frontier societies, how do they identity themselves and how do they interact with people outside of frontier? These are some of the important questions we are going to explore in the short but intensive intellectual tour over the Chinese frontier societies. This course provides two things to the students: first, for each of the major frontier societies in China, we will grip with the characteristic regional social dynamics by reading both scholarly works and some translated local documents. Students thus can get an overview of how each frontier society came into being and how the frontier populations conduct their cultural modes and belief systems, etc. This is a great way of knowing China in its reality. Second, students will be expected to compare the social dynamics from different Chinese frontiers and to relocate their own experiences of living in frontier societies outside China with the aids from the conceptual tools from this course. The trans-frontier comparisons will enable students to rethink the whole (China, in this case) in the lens of its constituents (the frontier societies) and vice versa.

Name: Introduction to International Business
Introduction:
1. Main elements:
As the most basic master's degree in international business, the course centres on economic analysis of the process of formation of an international business strategy and strengthens the theoretical component in the context of case analysis, using Strategy Star analysis.
2. Teaching objectives:
The course is designed to integrate theory and business practice closely into learning into the frontier dynamics of the subject and the latest international business practice activities, while enhancing management skills, broadening the perspective and shaping strategic thinking in international business.
3. Teaching modalities
Using the Northern Great Teaching Network http://course.pku.edu.cn/ teaching platform for classroom lectures, web exchanges, case discussions and literature reading
4. Performance appraisal
(1) Ordinary time: attendance, classroom participation, 30% (2) Case discussion and analysis: 35% (3) Reading and commentary: 35%

Name: Anticipatory Design Thinking
Introduction:
Design Thinking (DT) has emerged this decade as a powerful tool-kit to innovate in products, services and processes to stimulate creativity and become more competitive. This highly interactive workshop – by using a Co-work DT tournament- will help participants to become familiar, knowledgeable…and may be addict to DT.
OBJECTIVES OF THE WORKSHOP: To familiarize the MBA’s with the principles, methodology and success factors of Design Thinking as a tool to create and re-create the business model of a start-up or an existing company. To develop skills and attitudes to become “Design Thinkers” and experience the benefits of DT as a vehicle to become more competitive mainly in Digital Transformation.

Name: Entrepreneurship in China
Introduction:
Foreign entrepreneurs in China is fundamentally a course about entrepreneurship, through examples mostly from China and mostly from foreigners who have started businesses here. It will cover core entrepreneurial topics: legal issues, starting up, marketing, management, operations, strategy and finance.
The course objectives are to provide a foundation for future entrepreneurs and businesspeople who will need to work outside their native cultures.
The class will use case studies with required participation to work from examples to theory. The group project will be both analytic and practical, focused on real-world entrepreneurship.

Name: Quantitative Reasoning Methods
Introduction: This course is an introduction to methods of empirical social research, and how they are used to assemble, describe, and draw inferences from data. This course emphasizes on the most widely used statistical methods by social scientists, and how they can be applied to data from sample survey and archives.

Name: Ethnography and Modern Education
Introduction: Education has undergone various transformations in history which eventually resulted in the current form by which we call Modern Education. To illustrate such historicity of Modern Education, a few historical changes should be highlighted, including the institutional buildings of higher education i.e. universities since 19th century, the fact that education has been primarily organized along the science and humanistic goals, the division between college and research university, and so on. These historical transformations shed light on the trajectories of higher education undertaken in current societies. This course will provide with students a walk-through of the historical development of Modern Education, and the discussion of key themes in present education, using historical, sociological and ethnographic approaches. The key themes will include state and nation-building, morality, class, social distinction and mobility, elite education and leadership, symbolic boundaries and micro-power dynamic, and global diffusion of educational models. The discussion will be carried out with reference to real-life examples, cases, and experiences of China and other countries. As far as the dimension beyond China is concerned in this course, particularly the German, French and American models will be examined.

Name: Innovation and Economic Development Strategy
Introduction: Innovation is a fundamental driver of long-term economic development. For industrialized countries, how to maintain their own capacity for innovation, in particular their own national systems to support innovation, is particularly important for continued transformational progress in an era of globalization. For developing countries, industrial catch-up with developed countries was one of their top development priorities. However, what innovation is, how technological progress actually occurs, how it is regular, and what systems are more conducive to innovation and technological progress remains a long-standing concern for academia and policymakers. For our fellow students, understanding the mechanisms of micro-mechanisms in which innovation occurs and taking stock of experiences and lessons learned in the development history of each country are essential to their understanding of the problems and tasks prevailing in developing countries. The main objectives of this course are to provide students with basic knowledge and analytical methods of innovation and technological progress, to familiarize graduate students with the theoretical development context and the main issues in this field, to learn about the progress of scholars in related historical, theoretical and empirical research, and the controversy that still exists today among front-line scholars. The second objective was to enable students to gain a deeper understanding of the development problems of developing countries; to develop their own analytical and research capacities, thus laying the foundation for higher levels of academic research. The course is divided into three main sections, the first being the basic concepts, characteristics and analytical framework of innovation, and is based on the historical experience of the industrialized Western countries; the second being the classic theory of catch-up development and models of different schools. The third part is the industrial catch-up experience of East Asian countries, in which China ' s development will be discussed as a particularly important example. The course is taught in a combination of teaching by teachers and classroom discussions by teachers for three quarters of each session, followed by classroom discussions by students for one quarter. There are no textbooks for this course, and weekly reading materials are assigned, with a reading volume of about 80 pages per week. Reading materials are mainly derived from articles in academic journals and selected chapters of monographs. The content of the lectures is closely related to the content of the given reading, so that the pupils must complete the reading required for the week before the session. The results of this course are evaluated in three main sections, the first in the form of regular performance, the second in the form of intermediate examination results, and the third in the form of academic thesis. The first part, with 30 per cent of the results, examined primarily four points, i.e. attendance, whether the students had completed the prescribed reading material on time, i.e. whether the students were actively involved in the classroom discussions, and fourth, whether each student was generally scheduled to give one or two lectures per semester to the designated academic thesis, which was also included in the regular performance. Mid-term examinations accounted for 30 per cent of the results and were written answers to one volume. Final course thesis accounts for 40 per cent of the total.

Name: Rural China
Introduction: The " Rural China " course is an optional Chinese language course for students at the Yankyung College of Beijing University. Its purpose is to provide students with a systematic understanding of the history and current situation of rural and agricultural development in China and, in particular, of the transformation of the economic and social system in rural China since the establishment of the People ' s Republic of China. The course, in the form of a topic, addressed a wide range of key and topical issues in rural and agricultural development in China, such as the birth and evolution of the community system of rural people, the process and performance of responsible reform of rural households, the evolution and innovation of the rural financial system, the historical changes and recent developments of rural cooperative organizations, traditional rural governance and its modern transformation, the history and status of rural anti-poverty, and the past and future of agricultural civilization. Discussion of these issues provides a basis for a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of rural areas in China, which is one of the most important components of understanding the history and current situation of China as a whole.

Name: The Development of Chinese Civilization
Introduction: China has undergone unprecedented transformation in the recent decades. This course introduces students to three millenniums of Chinese history that fosters and shapes many changes and continuities. It illuminates the ways in which Chinese society had been organized and individual behaviors and rights molded. The course focuses on the themes that highlight the most important aspects of Chinese civilization in the past and points out how they continue to influence the present. These themes included: cosmology and political order, state and family, learning and society, ritual and religion, commerce and technology, ethnicity and identity, space and memory, as well as the Chinese interaction with the rest of the world. The course consists of lectures and seminar type discussions based on course readings. Students will also contribute by preparing shorter presentations on topics closely related to the central themes of the course.

Name: History of Chinese Art
Introduction: This course is designed to help the students understand the art of China. Emphasis will be placed on key monuments of painting, sculpture and architecture from the Shang to the Qing dynasties selected by virtue of their quality and historical significance. Individual works of art and major styles will be studied in their historical context and in relation to a broad cultural background. Lectures, readings, and discussions will introduce students to various systems of Chinese thought, modes of visual analysis, and art historical method.

Name: Economic Thinking of Chinese Business Managers
Introduction: In order to effectively manage, operate, and run a business in China, managers and executive leaders need to first understand the market conditions and the economic environment that they operate in. Is the “Fan Economy” taking over multinational consumer brands in China? If so, how can we leverage the power of a “Fan Economy” in China? Has the ideology behind Chinese businesses changed from “Channel is King” to “Product is King”? B (Baidu), A (Alibaba), and T (Tencent) are referred to as China’s “Big 3”. Baidu holds the power of search, Alibaba has the power of e-commerce, and Tencent has the power of social networking, However, will their positions now be threatened by the newly rising Chinese Tech Titans: T (Toutiao), M (Meituan), and D (Didi)? The economics theories presented in this course may be able to provide further insights on this.

Name: Chinese Politics in Historical Transition
Introduction: The curriculum is divided into the following areas: the political environment in China and the challenges it faces; the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party in transition; the formation and development of a socialist system of Chinese identity; a number of issues in China's system of government and State structures; a number of issues in China's political system reform and historical transformation; and new developments in Chinese politics since the eighteenth Congress.

Name: Studies in China's Foreign Economic Relations
Introduction:
China’s economic achievements depend on China’s policy of reform and openness, and the purpose of this course is to help students to understand the important components of China’s external openness – China’s external economic relations – which include issues such as China’s foreign trade, China’s foreign investment, Chinese OFDI, the renminbi exchange rate and internationalization, and China’s bilateral economic and trade relations with other countries. The purpose of the course is to develop the logical capacity and analytical framework for students to understand China ' s external economic relations and to help them judge and predict the future process of opening up China to the outside world.
Main teaching elements: 1, China ' s theory of foreign trade and comparative advantage; 2, China ' s relationship between foreign trade and China ' s economic growth; 3, China ' s introduction of foreign investment; 4, China ' s introduction of foreign investment and foreign trade; 5, China ' s trade and investment relations with the United States; 6, China ' s trade and investment relations with Japan; 7, China-EU trade and investment relations; 8, China ' s free trade area issues; 9, China ' s OFDI; 10, the internationalization of the renminbi exchange rate with the renminbi; 11, China ' s international influence on the economy.
Teaching requirements: The curriculum is presented and discussed in combination. Examinations: Study reports + class statements (40 per cent), final papers (60 per cent).

Name: Theory and Practice of International Development Assistance
Introduction: Course introduction: As economic power grows, China's responsibility to provide global “global public goods” also increases, including international humanitarian assistance, but mainly international development assistance. How and to what extent China should play these roles is important not only for the international community but also for China itself. Not only should China play these roles well in order to gain international recognition and reputation, but it should also learn to reconcile its interests while playing them. The future economic and political status of China in the world will depend critically on how it seeks to achieve both goals. These objectives are not necessarily in conflict with each other, but can be mutually reinforcing. Closely related to the increasing responsibility for global development and humanitarian assistance is the role that China will play in international financing for development and the global financial system. China’s recent and unexpected success in the establishment of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIB) is a testimony to China’s growing international financial influence and power. But China’s ultimate success on AIB will be measured by how it supports the economic and social development of the Asian region. While active participation in multilateral action is a way for China to become a regional and global provider of public goods, bilateral frameworks are another effective path and have so far led China ' s development and humanitarian assistance. However, on the basis of some value judgements, bilateral frameworks do not appear to be the preferred option for the international community, as aid parliaments are often seen as conditional on development aid for commercial gain from the recipient country. However, there is also good reason to believe that bilateral frameworks not only allow recipient countries to gain a sense of ownership of relevant aid projects, as in the case of multilateral aid frameworks, but also give donors a sense of ownership of the aid projects they finance. By involving the public in the donor country (social activists, non-profit organizations and civil society in general) in the monitoring and evaluation of projects, it will be beneficial to improve the design, implementation and management of development assistance projects. It could even facilitate a virtuous interaction among donors in the performance of development assistance projects. The current system of international development assistance led by the United Nations development organizations and the Bretton Woods institutions, including numerous regional development banks and other aid agencies, attached great importance to multilateralism and the role of multilateral institutions. However, there are many gaps in their management and accountability. While internal reforms may play a role, external monitoring and oversight are necessary. At present, the regulatory framework of many multilateral institutions makes it difficult to provide effective avenues for addressing these issues. On the contrary, it often leads to serious bureaucracy. The overall encouragement of the public participation of donor and host countries in the development assistance system can be an important force in improving the situation. Moreover, the current multilateral system places too much emphasis on expertise to ignore the importance of local knowledge. While there is no doubt that professional knowledge and skills are needed, these alone are far from sufficient. Technical solutions need to be fully integrated with local conditions and needs, which means that local knowledge is needed. The full participation of the public in the host country (active, non-profit organizations and civil society at large) in the decision-making and implementation process of development assistance projects will be the best way to acquire local knowledge (know what is possible, what is not, and what is urgently needed). Content and timing: 1. Theory and practice of international development assistance: introduction 2. A changing global development agenda, from the Millennium Goals to the Millennium Development Goals 3. Need for and importance of international development assistance (IDA) 4. Key IDA participants: Government, professional bodies, the public, non-profit organizations, social enterprises and the private sector 11. Course review Each of the above topics covers approximately one week of teaching time (2 hours). Teaching methods: The course will be taught in both lectures and classroom discussions. During two school hours a week, the first hour will be devoted to class discussions on the topics of the previous week ' s lectures, while the second hour will be introduced by the teacher on the next topic (theory, practice, case, research focus, etc.) and discussed in the next week ' s classroom (i.e. the first hour of two school hours). At the end of each lecture, students will be provided with reading material to allow them a week of reading, discussion and debate. The main reading materials for the course are listed below, while reading materials on specific topics are made available to students at the end of each lecture. Most reading materials will be in English. Depending on the number of students selected, classroom discussions can take the form of groups. If the selection is small, each student may have the opportunity to speak at each classroom discussion. In the event of a larger selection of subjects, discussion groups are divided according to the topic, each group leads the presentation on the topic of its choice, followed by a full-class discussion. Each student will be expected to be fully prepared for his or her lead statement, including through coordination or collaboration with other constituencies. Some lectures may invite other guests with a professional level of research in a given field.

Name: Contemporary Chinese Economic Development
Introduction: Contemporary economic development in China Course profile and curriculum Lecturer: Wang Sun-Gwan (Professor, Doctoral Teacher, School of Economics, Beijing University) Contact: 62757834 (Office), shuguang@pku.edu.cn Hours: 30 hours, 2 credits. Examination: 20 for classroom discussions, 30 for interim reporting and 50 for end-of-cycle reporting, 100 for total Question time: Thursday at 3 p.m., at the 408th office of the School of Economics Course introduction: The course on " Economic Development in Contemporary China " , an elective course offered by Professor Wang Sun Gwang to Masters and Doctors at the Faculty of Economics of Beijing University and relevant economic faculties, aims to systematically inform students of the history and current state of development of the contemporary Chinese economy and to systematically study and explore the characteristics and direction of the contemporary Chinese economy from the perspective of different disciplines, such as political economy, development economics, institutional economics, comparative economics and economic history. The course examines the underlying logic, historical experience and lessons of contemporary Chinese economic development in a combination of historical studies of economic development and thematic studies of economic development with an international perspective. The course covered a wide range of major topics, such as analysis of the long-term perspective of China ' s millennium economic growth, the formation and transformation of the socialist economic system, the exploration and transformation of the socialist market economy system, the transformation of the State enterprise system and innovation in State asset management, the transformation of the rural economic system and agricultural development, the process of China ' s distinctive industrialization and industrial structural transformation, the regional economic development strategy, the transformation of the economic growth model and the economic interpretation of China ' s miracles, the reform of China ' s financial system, the unbalanced characteristics of the Chinese economy and its direction. The courses, which have a strong historical depth and a degree of theoretical depth and frontier, are the basic courses of the Master ' s and Ph.D. studies in economics-related subjects to understand the Chinese economy. Teaching methods: (1) A combination of classroom lectures, panel discussions, field trips and lectures is used to enhance pupils ' overall understanding of and interest in the curriculum and enhance the effectiveness of classroom teaching in a variety of flexible forms.
